title: The London System
description: One of the most famous openings in chess, and for good reason. It is very easy to learn, and you can choose between slower paced games or vicious attacks on your opponent.

r1b2r2/ppqnbppk/4p3/2ppP3/5B1P/2P1P3/PP1.text:
Black has to take.

We will give a queen check on h5 to force the king back.

r1b2rk1/ppqnbpp1/4p3/2ppP2Q/5B1P/2P1P3/P.text: The king goes to g8. It has no choice.

r1b2rk1/ppqnbpp1/4p3/2ppP2Q/5B1P/2P1PN2/.text:
We have a massive kingside attack that will likely result in checkmate. 

Guess what? If 13...f6, you can still play Ng5!

r1b2rk1/ppqnbppp/4p3/2ppP3/5B1P/2PBP3/PP.text:
10...Qc7 is natural to attack the e5-pawn. 

However, we have a great sacrifice on h7. 

The engine is able to hold off checkmate, but your opponents aren't engines!

r1bq1r1k/pp1nb2p/4p1pQ/2ppPp2/5BPP/2PBP3.text:
Fear could be the reason black plays moves like this.

We can now break through.

r1bq1r1k/pp1nb2p/6pQ/2ppPp2/5B1P/2PBPN2/.text:
And that's all, folks. 

If checkmate is avoided, it will only be with Black giving up material, and even then the attack doesn't stop!

r1bq1r1k/pp1nb3/4ppQ1/2ppP3/5B1P/2P1P3/P.text:
Black moves away.

We'll force the king back to the g-file.

r1bq1r2/pp1nbppk/4p3/3pP3/2p2B1P/2P1P3/P.text:
Black must take.

Our queen will arrive on h5 with check!

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb1pp/4p3/2ppPp1Q/5B1P/2PBP3.text:
Black could have played that in one move!

Now we can play g4 right away, to great effect.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb1pp/4p3/2ppPp2/5B1P/2PBP3/.text: f5 is a lot more sound. It blocks the bishop's diagonal, and if we capture en passant Black will be able to bring the knight to f6 to defend the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb1pp/4p3/2ppPp2/5B1P/2PBPN2.text:
But we have Ng5 and g4 ideas to open up the kingside and attack. 

It's a fairly equal position, but Black  will have to defend.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb1pp/4pp2/2ppP3/5B1P/2PBP3/.text:
f6 is highly popular here and it must be considered. Additionally, it's not as bad as playing some random move like 10...Re8.

But it's still bad. We will go on the attack with Qh5, hitting h7!

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb2p/4p1p1/2ppPp1Q/5BPP/2PBP.text:
Black may try to put pressure on our queen.

But we can open the position before they can harass us further.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb2p/4ppp1/2ppP2Q/5B1P/2PBP3.text:
g6 is a common blunder.

We will simply sacrifice on g6, opening up the king's defenses.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb3/4pp1Q/2ppP3/5B1P/2P1P2R/.text:
And this gives our rook a chance to give check on the g-file. 

Black is lost.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nb3/4ppp1/2ppP2Q/5B1P/2P1P3/.text:
Black captures.

We'll take, giving check.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpp1/4p3/3pP2Q/2p2B1P/2P1PN.text: And Ng5 can't be stopped, since even if black goes f6, we can play Ng5 as we'll open up our h-file and get a pawn on g6. Black's king is not surviving for long.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4p3/2ppP3/5B2/2PBP3/PP.text:
Retreating to d7, to keep an eye on the e5 pawn.

We will begin a pawn storm with h4!

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4p3/3pP3/2p2B1P/2PBP3/.text:
Black could try to gain space in the queenside while gaining a tempo on the bishop.

But this allows us to play the Greek gift bishop sacrifice!

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PBPN.text:
Black castles.

And we'll advance our knight into e5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2ppn3/3P1B2/2PBP3/.text:
Taking the knight immediately is popular but probably not a good idea.

Just remember to recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN2.text:
Black places their bishop on a very natural square and prepares castling.

We'll put our bishop on d3 where it stares at h7.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
Black brings their knight out...

And so will we. Notice how we control the e5 square very well. This is another idea in the London.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPPN.text:
After black undermines our d4 pawn...

We support our central structure by adding another protector with c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

e3 is part of our ideas in this opening. The point is to get a c3/d4/e3 structure.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black opens up their dark-squared bishop.

We develop our knight. We haven't been forced to play c3 just yet.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

And we bring our bishop out to f4. This is the London.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first chapter of this course! Congratulations on beginning this journey! 

First things first, we'll go over a very common line in the London. Black will develop their Bishop to e7, a very natural square. And we're going to learn our new reliable moves that will almost always be available to us in the London!

We begin with 1.d4.

r1b1r1k1/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/2ppN3/3P4/2PBP1B.text:
If they take us with 9...Bxe5, 10.dxe5 establishes a powerful e5-pawn that will be supported and defended. Black therefore simply attacks us. 

We will support the knight by playing f4.

r1b1r1k1/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/3pN3/3p1P2/2PBP1.text:
With nothing else to do, Black may interject this capture. 

We will capture with the e-pawn so that they don't get any ...Nb4 moves, harassing our d3-bishop.

r1b1r1k1/ppqn1ppB/2nbp3/3pN3/3P1P2/2P3B1.text:
Check! A Greek Gift! 

The rook on e8 lacks a defender. Black will lose it if they take our bishop!

r1b1r1k1/ppqn1ppp/2nbp3/3pN3/3P1P2/2PB2B.text: This move is a fatal mistake.

r1bq1r1k/p3bNpB/1pn1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2P3n1/P.text: We've got this check, attacking the queen too.

r1bq1r1k/p3bppB/1pn1p3/2ppP1N1/3P4/2P3n1.text:
And after the king moves...

We've got this crafty intermezzo, attacking the queen too.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1pn1p3/2ppP1N1/3P4/2PB2n.text:
Taking our bishop isn't a good idea...

We'll capture on h7 with check.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1pn1p3/2ppP2n/3P4/2PB1NB.text:
The knight should go after the bishop, by all means.

Now we have an interesting move. We give up the knight but open up an attack on black's knight and possibly h7.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1pn1pn2/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1NB.text:
Bringing the bishop back should be played.
 
We can now create some discomfort for Black by pushing forward with e5.

r1bq1rk1/p4p1p/1pn1p1p1/2ppP1bQ/3P4/2PB2.text:
Blocking the mate threat on h7.

We will retreat the queen to e2 and defend the knight.

r1bq1rk1/p4p1p/1pn1p1p1/3pP1b1/3p4/2PB2B.text:
So we're sacrificing a pawn, but...

We will attack with h4.

r1bq1rk1/p4p1p/1pn1p1pb/3pP2P/8/2pB2B1/P.text:
Black can always insert this capture.

We will take back.

r1bq1rk1/p4p1p/1pn1p1pb/3pP3/3p3P/2PB2B1.text:
The bishop retreats, still with an eye towards our knight.

We'll continue our attack, pushing forward with h5.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/1pn1p1p1/3pP2P/8/2PB2B1/P.text:
Black gets the bishop off the h-file, as we were threatening hxg6, discovering an attack on the bishop.

We'll prepare to castle by hand.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/1pn1p1p1/4P2P/2Pp4/3B2B1/.text: c4 is reliable, keeping the center closed. We also get the e4 square. The position is complicated. We are down a pawn, but the black king faces a strong attack.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/1pn1p1p1/4P2P/3p4/2PB2B1/.text: If d4, trying to open up the position...

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/1pn1p3/2ppP1bn/3P4/2PB2B1.text:
If Black takes our knight (the best move)...

We will capture on h5.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/1pnbp3/2p5/3Pn3/2PB1NB1/P.text:
Black alleviates the pressure by trading.

We recapture and attack the remaining knight.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/1pnbpn2/2p5/3Pp3/2PB1NB1/.text:
This is the most popular move... but it's not correct.

We can just take with the knight, attacking the d6 bishop.

r1bq1rk1/p4ppp/1pnbpn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNB1/.text:
b6 defends the c5 pawn. Additionally, it allows the light-squared bishop to develop.

We'll break in the center, threatening e5!

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PNB1/.text:
A very standard move. Castling is important in every opening.

We'll bring our light-squared bishop to d3, eyeing h7.

r1bq3k/p3brpB/1pn1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2P3P1/PP1.text: We've got a powerful discovered check coming right up.

r1bq3k/p3brpB/1pn1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2P3n1/PP1.text: Black more or less has to capture..

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN2/.text:
Now this is the point of the variation: Black proposes a bishop trade. Naturally, we won't comply.

Let's bring the bishop back. If they take, they open up our h-file! 

7...Qc7 is a mistake that allows 8.dxc5, and 7...Bxg3 gives us the open h-file! Already two ways Black can go wrong!

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PNB1/P.text:
Let's bring the bishop back. If they take, they open up our h-file! 

7...Qc7 is a mistake that allows 8.dxc5, and 7...Bxg3 gives us the open h-file! Already two ways Black can go wrong!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
They develop the queenside knight.

And we develop our kingside knight!

r1bqr1k1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNB1/.text:
Black may want to push ...e5 here. 

But we can stop them by jumping our knight into e5.

r2q1rk1/pb3ppp/1pn1p3/2b5/Q3B3/2P2NB1/PP.text:
We gain a tempo on the knight! Many things to consider here.  13...Qe8 or 13...Qc8 allow the 14.Bxh7+ Greek Gift!

Maybe best is 13...Na5, when 14.Rd1 Qc8 15.Bd3 follows. Our queen can swing over to h4.

Finally, the defense with 13...Rc8 allows us 14.Rd1. Black has to be wary of attacks on their bishops.

r2q1rk1/pb3ppp/1pnbp3/2p5/3PB3/2P2NB1/PP.text:
Black defends the knight.

But we take the c-pawn, attacking the d6-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPPN.text:
Black undermines d4.

We'll support our center with c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we play e3, consolidating our structure.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black goes e6 themselves.

We'll develop the b1-knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We'll develop our bishop to f4, before playing e3!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, you'll be introduced to a very natural idea from black: playing Bd6 to try and fight for control of e5 and try to trade the bishops. The moves in here are pretty natural for black, so the chances to actually get this either by preparation or luck are pretty high. Let's get on with it! We open with 1.d4.

r1b2rk1/p1qn1ppp/1p1bpn2/2pp4/1PPP4/4PNB.text:
Again, we're opening up the c-file for our rook. Pawn tension on this file benefits us while the queen remains on the c-file. 

We have ideas of cxd5 to create a pin.

The bishop will come out to e2, since on d3 it may be attacked by a knight after trades on c5.

r1b2rk1/p1qn1ppp/1p1bpn2/2pp4/2PP4/4PNB1.text:
Black may support the c5-pawn with ...b6. 

However, this doesn't get rid of the x-ray along the c-file.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PNB1/.text:
Developing the knight and controlling e5 with another piece.

We're going to open up the c-file for our rook! 

With the queen on c7, the idea behind our setup is to create some discomfort for Black.

rnb2rk1/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PNB1/P.text:
And now Black increases pressure on e5.
 
We can bring the rook to x-ray the queen.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1P1B1/P.text:
Black castles right away.

We'll play Ngf3 to control e5.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/PP.text:
Offering to trade bishops.

We reject it. We only want to trade on our terms.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPPN.text:
Black goes c5.

And we support our central d4 pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text: Black develops their knight. We'll continue with e3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black plays e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop. 

We bring our b1-knight out.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text: Black mirrors us, and we bring our bishop out!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Black may have some other ideas under their sleeve. Specifically, bringing the bishop out to d6 at an earlier time. However, there can still be a transposition to the main line. 

So, what to look for? Well, a setup with c5 without Nc6, and the bishop on d6 and queen on c7. Let's see how to combat this! 

We open with the queen's pawn.

r1bq1rk1/p3b2p/1pn1ppp1/2pp3n/3P3B/2PBPN.text:
Black castles kingside. 

Like I said, even though the pawns have been pushed to the 6th rank, the king is safe.

r1bq1rk1/p3b2p/1pn1ppp1/2pp3n/3PP2B/2PB1.text:
And now e4. We should be doing alright here.

We haven't gotten a winning advantage by any means, but both sides should enjoy having achieved what they wanted. 

We have ideas of exd5 to open up our rook.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p1p/2nbp1p1/3p3n/3P4/2PNB3/P.text:
Black castles.

Now g3 is a nice move to castle and control f4 and also enable Bg2.

r1bq1rk1/pp5p/2nbp1p1/3p1p1n/3P4/2PNB1P1.text:
If Black should go wrong, we'll change plans of course.

This looks very natural but it allows us to gain multiple tempi on the Black pieces while improving our own pieces. Firstly, we'll attack the f8-rook.

r1bqk2r/p3b2p/1pn1ppp1/2pp3n/3P3B/2PBPN2.text:
Black usually goes for a fianchetto.

And White, like in many London positions, can orchestrate e4.

r1bqk2r/pp2b2p/2n1ppp1/2pp3n/3P3B/2PBPN2.text:
Black unpins their f-pawn.

Even though the kingside pawns have been pushed, this engine-approved variation for Black is safe enough because there isn't an immediate way to exploit the pawns on the 6th rank.

We'll castle and further our development.

r1bqk2r/pp3p1p/2nbp1p1/3pN2n/3P4/2P1B3/P.text:
Black defends the knight.

We will retreat because our knight didn't have enough support on e5. 

Nevertheless, we're still aiming to maintain control over e5.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nbp3/3p3n/3P4/2P1BN2/PP1.text:
Black finally develops the f8-bishop.

We'll play Ne5, a discovered attack on the h5-knight.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/3P4/2P2NB1/PP1.text: Allows us to simply retreat and keep control over e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2pp3n/3P1B2/2P1PN2.text:
Attacking the bishop right away is an option.

Let's attack the queen.

We want to provoke some weaknesses before potentially trading the bishop off.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p3n/3P1B2/2P2N2/P.text:
And now Black gains a tempo, attacking our bishop.

We will drop it back to e3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
Black develops. We do likewise.

Now we will explore the details associated with not developing the f8-bishop so quickly. Black can go after our bishop with ...Nh5 ideas.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3p1B2/2P1PN2/.text:
Black can insert this capture.

We will recapture with the e-pawn, retaining control over the b4 square.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2n1pp2/2pp2Bn/3P4/2P1PN2/.text:
f6 blocking and attacking our bishop.

We'll step back to h4.

r1bqkb1r/pp5p/2n1ppp1/2pp3n/3P3B/2P1PN2/.text:
Supporting the knight.

We'll develop the bishop. 

After Black has gone for ...Nh5 and ...g6, it seems our bishop bites on granite on g6. Thus Black's setup, while not intuitive, makes some sense in that it makes our bishops less effective.

r1bqr1k1/pp5p/2nbp1pB/3p1p1n/3P4/2PN2P1/.text:
Getting out of the way.

We'll block the e-file and attack the knight with Be2.

r1bqr1k1/pp5p/2nbpnpB/3p1p2/3P4/2PN1NP1/.text:
And we can gain control of e5 quite nicely! 

We also have plans of h4 and h5 if the knight ever moves from f6, and, of course, we're getting a knight on e5 ourselves.

r1bqr1k1/pp5p/2nbpnpB/3p1p2/3P4/2PN2P1/P.text: The knight goes back to f6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPPN.text:
Now Black goes for an early c5.

We'll support our central pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black goes Nf6, standard stuff. 

We play e3 now that the bishop is out.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black plays e6, supporting their center.

We develop our b1-knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We'll bring our bishop out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to a very important study on Black choosing not to develop the Bishop on f8 immediately. What if Black plays all the normal moves of the Nf6/e6 setup, but chooses to attack the bishop early with something like Nh5? Let's see exactly what can happen in these positions. 

Let's begin with 1.d4.

lessons.title: Black Plays d5, c5, Nf6, Nc6

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn2np1/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.text:
Black will fianchetto. 

...Bf5, supported by the g6-pawn, is another idea.

But we can go for the e4 break.

This move is good because it will end up weakening the c4-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn3p1/3p4/2pPnB2/2P5/P.text:
Black could take.

We'll simply recapture.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3.text:
Targeting our b-pawn.

We'll block the attack, proposing a queen trade to open up the a-file.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/1QP1P.text:
Black wants to pressure us into trading on b6. 

Of course, we don't want to activate their rook, so we just go back to c2, preparing to undermine the c4-pawn by playing e4.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
Black develops their knight.

We continue in a standard way by developing our knight. 

After ...c5 and ...Nc6, we want to go for queenside development because we want to be able to answer ...Qb6.

Moves like 5. Nf3 would be inaccurate.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3p1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
An alternative is exchanging pawns.

We'll recapture with the e-pawn as we would like to retain control over b4.

r1q1k2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB1N.text:
Black develops the bishop.

And we castle.

r1q1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QP5/P.text:
Black defends their b-pawn.

We'll continue to develop.

r1q1kb1r/pp3pp1/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1B2/1QP5/P.text:
Black recaptures.

Even though the h-file opens up,  the h2-pawn isn't so weak because of our London bishop.

We'll develop our bishop to its best diagonal.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p4/3PnB2/1QP2N2/P.text: We just come back. We're going to calmly play Bd3 and 0-0, and claim that Black's queen on c8 doesn't achieve much. White is better.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QP2N.text:
Defending.

Now we go after the f5-bishop.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QP2N2.text:
Consolidating the central pawn structure.

We will place our bishop on the long diagonal.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3PbB1N/1QP5/P.text:
Black goes to a square where the bishop is defended by the knight.

Now we can simply win the bishop pair.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/8/3PpB1N/1QP3P1/P.text: We'll use g2 for our knight, e2 for our bishop, and castle. Then we'll open the position for our bishop pair with f3.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/8/3PpB1N/1QP5/PP3.text: The idea is to take away our f3 square.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pnb1/3p4/3P1B1N/1QP5/.text:
Black retreats.

We'll claim the bishop pair.

r1q2rk1/1p2bpp1/p1n1pnp1/3p4/3P1B2/2PB4/.text: But we're going to start transferring pieces to the kingside. Then we can even push the pawns in front of our king, given that all our pieces are there!

r1q2rk1/pp2bpp1/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1B2/1QPB4/.text:
Black castles.

We'll transfer the a-rook to the semi-open e-file.

r1q2rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB1N.text:
Castling is natural, and popular here.

But it allows us to gain a tempo on the bishop by playing Ne5.

r1q2rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3pN2b/3P1B2/1QPB1.text:
We can bring our other knight to the party and we stand slightly better. 

We'll want to bring our a-rook into the e-file, although rook from f to e1 is also fine. Leaving the rook on f1 is often good in case we go for f4 ideas after moving the pieces away from the f-file.

r1q2rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3pN2b/3P1B2/1QPB4.text: If Black gets out of the way...

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P5/PP.text:
The option of developing the bishop is always present.

In reply, we'll develop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/2P5/PP1.text:
The bishop can also be developed with a tempo on our queen.

But we gain a tempo right back by hitting b7.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2/.text:
Black prepares to develop their dark-squared bishop.

We attack the b-pawn.

r3kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn3p1/3p1b2/2pPNB2/2P2P2.text:
It's not going to go well for them.

Black will have to take on e4, and we'll recapture with a strong pawn in the center, plus the fact that c4 will be weak.

r3kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn3p1/3p1b2/2pPNB2/2P5/P.text: And if Black wants to be tricky...

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/2pP1Bb1/2P1P3/.text:
The bishop is developed with the idea it may make its way to g6.

We'll target the c4-pawn immediately by playing b3.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1pP1P3/.text:
Black takes.

We recapture and open up our rook.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/3p4/1P1P1Bb1/2P1P3.text:
We expand on the queenside! 

We'll continue with standard piece development (Bd3, Ngf3), but we also have b5 to remove the knight from c6 and get our knight to e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black undermines our center.

Of course we will play c3 and support it.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

We'll play e3 now that the bishop is out.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We'll develop the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to Chapter 2! In this chapter we'll see what Black can do if they choose not to play e6 right away. With that extra tempo, they could even develop the light-squared bishop before blocking it behind the pawn chain. 

Black still will play d5/Nf6/c5/Nc6, just that on move 5 they'll have many options. Let's open with 1.d4, and explore further!

r1bk1b1r/pp1npppp/5n2/8/4pB2/2N5/PPP1NPP.text: Even though queens are off the board, our lead in development and Black's exposed king gives us an advantage. We will soon regain the pawn by playing Ng3.

r1bk1b1r/pp1npppp/5n2/8/4pB2/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: Black blocks the check and develops a piece at the same time.

r3kb1r/pp1n2pp/4pn2/2p5/4pB2/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: Despite being down a pawn, we are better. We are ahead in development and will win back the pawn on e4 soon by bringing our g1 knight to g3, leaving Black with a weakness on e6.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4pn2/1BpP4/4pB2/2N5/PP.text:
The most obvious interposition. Even though it looks like the bishop is both blocking the check and defending the e6 pawn, the latter is an illusion.

We take on e6, and because of the pin to the king, Black cannot recapture with their bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pp1b2pp/4pn2/1Bp5/4pB2/2N5/PPP2.text:
The only way Black can recapture, as we noted.

We'll trade off bishops.

rn2kb1r/pp1q2pp/4pn2/2p5/4pB2/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
This recapture makes sense. Black is behind in development and proposes a queen trade.

We have no way of avoiding the endgame, but actually it is okay for us, in spite of being down a pawn for the moment.

rnbk1b1r/pp2pppp/5n2/8/4pB2/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black defends the e4 pawn.

Let's castle with check!

rnbk1bnr/pp2pppp/8/8/4pB2/8/PPP2PPP/RN2K.text:
Black recaptures the queen.

We'll attack the e4 pawn and get ready to castle queenside.

rnbqk2r/1p2ppbp/p4np1/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPP1.text:
Black develops their bishop and gets ready to castle.

We'll finally recapture the sacrificed pawn.

rnbqk2r/1p2ppbp/p5p1/2pP4/4QB2/8/PPP2PPP.text: We recapture and have good attacking chances. The open e-file may also be relevant once we connect our rooks. We will definitely consider advancing our h-pawn in the near future.

rnbqk2r/1p2ppbp/p5p1/2pP4/4nB2/8/PPP1QPP.text: Black trades off a pair of knights.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pp1p/p4np1/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black gets ready to develop the kingside bishop to g7.

We castle, placing our rook on a great square. It guards our d5 pawn and is opposite the Black queen.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPP2.text:
A clever move - Black realizes that a bishop check on b5 would be annoying, so denies us access to that square.

We'll get ready to win back the e4 pawn and also to castle queenside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPP2.text: If Black realizes that e6 is a mistake, they may instead opt to fianchetto their bishop, just like White often does in the standard Albin countergambit.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPPQ.text: We have a very easy attack. When Black plays Bg7, we will be ready to trade it off with Bh6. We can castle queenside next and start an attack by advancing our h pawn, which is often an effective strategy against fianchettos.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pP4/4pB2/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black develops their knight and attacks our important d5 pawn.

5.Nc3 is the only reasonable way of guarding our attacked d5 pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pP4/4pB2/2N5/PPP2P.text:
It's a mistake when white plays e3 in the Albin in the corresponding position there, and it's a mistake here for the same reason!

We will check on b5! When Black blocks the check, they will be unable to recapture on e6 with their bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3PpB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black accepts our gambit, in the style of the Albin.

We move our pawn forward, securing a space advantage.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
Black can attack our center at this very early juncture.

With our reply of 3.e4, we are essentially playing an Albin countergambit (1. d4 d5 2. c4 c5), but since we are White, we have the extra move Bf4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3pPB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The other way of capturing.

We will recapture with the queen, also attacking Black's d5 pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/8/3QpB2/8/PPP2PPP/RN2.text:
The only logical follow-up - otherwise we will take on d5.

Even though we're down a pawn for the moment, the endgame will be fine for us. We're ahead in development and black will find it difficult to keep the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. This is one of Black's two most common responses.

We bring our bishop to a great square. This is the start of the London.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the Reverse Albin! If you've bought the Black Gambits Repertoire (you should, what are you waiting for?) you'll know that the Albin is a very good practical weapon. 

Here, when Black plays 2. c5, we'll gambit a pawn in the center and go for similar ideas as in the Albin. 

We begin our opening with 1.d4.

1rbqkb1r/5ppp/1p2pn2/1BPp4/1P6/4P3/P4PPP.text: This check is very hard to meet. If black blocks the check with a piece on d7, then c6 will win material. After Ke7, we will still play c6 with a crushing position.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p1n2n2/qBPp4/5B2/2N1P3/.text:
If we are attacked with a6...

Just take the knight.

r1b1kb1r/4p1pp/p1p2p2/2Pp4/5B2/2P1PN2/P1.text:
Black wants to play e5 and shut our bishop down.

We'll play Bc7! It keeps our bishop alive and active even after e5 is played.

r1b1kb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/2qp4/5B2/2N1PN2/PP.text:
The queen captures the pawn.

We will continue by placing a knight in the center.

r1b1kb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/q1Pp4/5B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
When Black recaptures...

Our superior development should yield some form of advantage for us.

r1b1kb1r/4pppp/p1p5/2Pp4/5B2/2q1PN2/PPP2.text: And after a series of trades...

r1b1kb1r/4pppp/p1p5/q1Pp4/3Q1B2/2n1PN2/P.text:
Black could liquidate.

Let's accept the trades.

r1b1kb1r/4pppp/p1p5/q1Pp4/4nB2/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Attacking c5 and the knight on c3!
 
We will respond with Qd4, defending.

r1b1kb1r/5ppp/p1p1pn2/2qpN3/5B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
e6 is a popular move in these positions.

We will castle. We stand slightly better because Black's bishop on c8 is not a very good piece.

r1b1kb1r/5ppp/p1p1pn2/q1Pp4/5B2/2N1PN2/P.text:
Play could continue with the solid e6.

Then castling has the additional benefit of unpinning our knight.

r1b1kb1r/6pp/pBp2p2/2Ppp3/8/2P1PN2/P1P2P.text: But we won't have a single bad piece in the resulting endgame. We have Nd2 and c4 to look forward to.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2qp4/5B2/4PN2/PPP.text: Black develops their knight and acquires some control over the e5 square.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2qp4/5B2/P3PN2/1P.text: We are ready to expand on the queenside with b4 and c4 next. We are already ahead in development and Black will have to lose more time moving their queen.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/qBPp4/5B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Black could give a check, which in turn is also attacking the bishop!

That's why we must block the check and defend the bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/qBPp4/4nB2/P1N1P3/.text:
But not in this one. If Nxc3 we can just recapture with our knight and everything is defended.

b4 is a threat, so capturing the c5-pawn won't be easy.
Complicating matters might be a good solution in certain scenarios...

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/qBPp4/5B2/2N1P3/P.text:
...e6 this early on is not good. It blocks the bishop in and is not effective in recovering the pawn.

We'll play a3, when Bxc5 fails to b4, forking queen and bishop.

r1b2rk1/3qbppp/2p1pn2/p1Pp4/1P1N1B2/2P1P.text: And we castle. We'll have a nice game holding on to the extra pawn.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/2n1pn2/pBPp4/1P3B2/2P1P.text:
Castling.

Let's take on c6. This prevents b6 from ever happening.

r1bq1rk1/4bppp/2p1pn2/p1Pp4/1P3B2/2P1PN2.text:
Black now has a new c-pawn, and b6 undermining our structure will never happen.

Our knight can now hop into the center and attack c6.

r1bqk2r/1p2bppp/2n1pn2/pBPp4/1P3B2/2P1P3.text:
Again, when you see this alternative move, just realize it's too slow.

We'll just develop too, while holding on to the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/2n1pn2/p1Pp4/1P3B2/2P1P3.text:
Putting more pressure on our queenside - we have to do something about the attack on the b4 pawn.

We'll develop, and deal with the attack on our b4 pawn by pinning the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2Pp4/5B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
This is the most popular move.

I suggest we pin the knight.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1p1p/2n1p1p1/pBPp4/PP3N2/1QP.text: We keep a strong queenside. Remember to go Ra2 after Bg7.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n1p3/1BPp4/1P2nB2/1Q2P.text: But we prepare to block with Nbc3.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n1p3/pBPp3n/1P3B2/1QP1.text:
Black can go for the bishop pair.

We'll get ready to capture with a piece, by playing 9.Ne2.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n1p3/pBPp4/1P2nB2/1QP1.text:
Black places the knight on an active square.

We kick it out right away.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n1p3/pBPp4/1P3n2/1QP1P.text: Black takes, and we'll recapture with the knight.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n1pn2/pBPp4/1P3B2/2P1P.text:
So Black unpins.

We'll protect b4 once again. The game is still complicated, but we are up a pawn and not in any immediate danger.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n5/pBPp4/1P2Pp2/1QP1P3.text:
Black takes.

We'll take on d5, with a huge center. Black will have to play actively and creatively to stay in the game.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n5/pBPpp3/1P2nB2/1QP1P.text:
Black plays actively and complicates matters; after all, they are a pawn down!

But this trade is favorable.

r3k2r/1b2bppp/p1p1pn2/q2pN3/NPP2B2/4P3/P.text: We can gain another tempo on the queen. The idea is Rb1 if the pawn is taken.

r3kb1r/1b3ppp/p1p1pn2/2qpN3/5B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
Attempting to improve the bishop...

But we can gain a tempo on the queen.

r3kb1r/1b3ppp/p1p1pn2/q2pN3/N4B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Black retreats, attacking the knight...

But c4 undermines the center and opens up a defense on our knight!

r3kb1r/1p1b1ppp/2n5/pBPP4/1P3p1q/1QP1P3/.text: We will move to d1. The most challenging move to meet will be ...Qf2, when we need to find Ne2, with a complex position.

r3kb1r/3b1ppp/p1p1pn2/2qp4/5B2/P1N1PN2/1.text:
The queen captures...

We will gain a tempo on the queen with the knight.

r3kb1r/3b1ppp/p1p1pn2/q1Pp4/5B2/2N1PN2/P.text:
The bishop trapped behind the pawns is bad in these positions.

After we play a3, Black must take on c5 while they can!

r3kb1r/q2b1ppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/N1P2B2/P3PN2/.text:
Undermining the center works well to keep our advantage! 

We have ideas of Ne5 and b4 if allowed. If ...dxc4, Ne5 and Nxc4 should be our plan to control the d6-square even further.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2qp4/5B2/4P3/PPPN1P.text:
Black recaptures the pawn on c5.

We'll continue developing our pieces.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/q1Pp4/5B2/4P3/PPP2P.text:
This does win back the pawn for Black, but clearly taking on c5 with the queen isn't as good as taking with the bishop would be.

We block the check by bringing our knight to d2. We don't play Nc3, because then it would be a target for a ...Ne4 by Black.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P3B2/P3P3/2P.text: And we've got normal development, plus we have preserved the extra pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P3B2/4P3/P1P2.text:
This, for example, is too slow.

We can connect all our pawns here.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1p3B2/2P1P3/P4.text:
Capturing is natural.

We recapture. Logical, logical, as GM Hikaru would say.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/4pn2/p1Pp4/1P3B2/4P3/P1P.text:
Black should try to challenge our queenside structure immediately. Otherwise, we will consolidate by playing a3 and simply be up a pawn.

We protect the pawn. We cannot play a3 instead because of the pin on the a file.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/1p2pn2/2Pp4/1P3B2/4P3/P4PP.text:
This is a standard idea in some similar positions. Black wants to regain the pawn using the pin of the c5 pawn to the b4 pawn. However, it fails here for tactical reasons.

We will want to check on b5, but first we remove a defender from Black's queenside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
It's very common for Black to make this pawn break in the London. They can try it here, or even as early as the previous move.

While Black will get some compensation, we can actually take this pawn. It isn't easy for them to recover the pawn with their bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/5B2/4P3/PPP2PP.text: With the idea of playing Bxc5 next, if allowed, so we prevent it by playing b4!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black brings the g8 knight to the most natural square and starts developing the kingside.

We reinforce our d4 pawn and get ready to develop our other bishop in the future.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. This is one of Black's two most common responses.

We bring our bishop to a great square. This is the start of the London.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second study of this chapter. Again, we'll be facing an early c5 from Black. In this case, we'll utilize a very easy-to-remember and practical weapon: simply taking on c5! In some situations, you'll see we'll even be able to hold on to the pawn!

Once again, we will open with 1.d4.

r1b1k2r/p4ppp/1pnqpn2/2pp4/3P1P2/2PBP3/P.text:
...b6 is often played to develop the bishop. 

We'll bring our other knight to f3.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2nqpn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBP3/PP1.text:
Black recaptures.

And boom! We enter our Stonewall by playing f4.

We're going for total control of e5, where we'll eventually jump a knight into.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3p1P2/2PBP3/PP.text:
Black can insert this capture to weaken our pawn grip. We'll take back on d4 with the c-pawn, otherwise we would lose the pawn on f4.

The c-file is now open.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PBP3/P.text:
And when Black proposes the trade of bishops...

We will, unusually for the London system, accept.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
Black develops their knight.

We'll bring our king's bishop to the active post on d3.

r3k2r/pb3ppp/1pnqpn2/2pp4/3P1P2/2PBPN2/P.text:
A very logical continuation. b6 was played to fianchetto, after all.

We will leap our knight into e5!

r3k2r/pp1b1ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P1P2/3BP3/PP1.text:
Developing the bishop.

We'll play a3 to prevent the Black knight from jumping into b4.

r3qrk1/pp2n1pp/2b1p3/3p1p1Q/3P1P2/P2BPN2.text:
Black offers a queen trade to ease the pressure.

In some positions, we would decline, but here we are leaving Black with markedly inferior minor pieces, thus the ending is very promising for us.

r3r1k1/pp2n1pp/2b1p3/3p1p2/3P1P2/P2BPN2/.text:
And we're first on the c-file! Our knight will also be very powerful on e5! Black's bishop looks like a big pawn!

We can go for doubling rooks on the c-file, and we will make use of the fact that we're quicker than Black in reaching key squares with our pieces.

r4rk1/pb2nppp/1p1qpn2/2ppN3/3P1PP1/2PBPQ.text:
Our queen is joining the attack! 

We can go for attacking ideas such as g5 and Qh3. The knight on f6 can't jump into e4 because we just take the material and consolidate the pawn up advantage if that happens.

r4rk1/pb3ppp/1pnqpn2/2ppN3/3P1P2/2PBP3/P.text:
Black castles.

We start attacking with g4!

r4rk1/pp1b1ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P1P2/P2BP3/1P.text:
Black castles.

Our knight has to come to f3 in these structures.

r4rk1/pp1bnppp/3qpn2/3p4/3P1P2/P2BPN2/1P.text:
A standard defensive maneuver.

We'll castle.

r4rk1/pp1nn1pp/2bqp3/3pNp1Q/3P1P2/P2BP3/.text:
Black could try to block the dangerous diagonal.

We'll exchange on d7, forcing one of Black's well-placed pieces to retreat and capture.

r4rk1/pp1nnppp/2bqp3/3pN3/3P1P2/P2BP3/1P.text:
Black challenges our knight on e5. 

We attack h7 and threaten mate. An idea can be the rook lift with Rf3-h3!

r4rk1/pp1qn1pp/2b1p3/3p1p1Q/3P1P2/P2BP3/.text:
The queen takes.

Now we plan to get our remaining knight to the e5 outpost.

r4rk1/pp2nppp/2bqpn2/3p4/3P1P2/P2BPN2/1P.text:
The bishop goes to c6 now that the knight has vacated that square.

And now our knight reaches e5!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPPN.text:
After c5 undermining our structure...

We'll support our center with c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

We'll reply with e3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
And Black plays e6.

We'll reply by developing our knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. 

We'll develop the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Hello there! This is perhaps the most important bonus weapon of them all. The Stonewall arising from the London. 

Arriving at it will include a slight variation in the move order, however, as we had been used to Ngf3 on move 6, but in this instance, we're leaving the f-pawn available. Let's start with 1.d4, and see exactly how!

2r1kb1r/1p2pppp/p1n2nb1/1BPp4/3N1B2/2P1P.text:
If Black attempts to force matters...

We will take on c6 and put pressure on the weak queenside pawns.

2r1kb1r/4pppp/p1p2nb1/2Pp4/3N1B2/2P1P3/P.text: Black recaptures, and now they  have weaknesses on a6 and c6.

2r1kb1r/4pppp/p1p2nb1/2Pp4/Q2N1B2/2P1P3/.text:
And we can even enter piece sacrifice territory. 

If ...Qxd2, Qxa6 attacks the rook and puts pressure on the c6-pawn, which would fall with check. It's hard to find a safe square for the rook!

2r1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2nb1/1BPp4/3N1B2/2P1P3.text:
The most played move.

However, it allows us to simply castle and place greater pressure on Black's position. For example...

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we'll continue in standard fashion with Nd2.

r1q1kb1r/pp3pp1/2n1pnp1/2pp4/3P1B2/1QP1P.text:
We neutralize the h-file and also create a retreat square for our bishop.

Our bishop will be developed to e2 and we'll play 0-0.  We can gain space with a4 and placing rooks on the c- and d-files is always a good plan.
Black recaptures and opens up the h-file.

r1q1kb1r/pp3pp1/2n1pnp1/2pp4/3P1BP1/1QP1.text: The h-file is opened for the rook. We had better not fall for any tricks with Nxg4!

We fianchetto. The bishop holds the kingside together. It will be unopposed, so we will have the bishop pair advantage. 

We'll of course castle kingside and then place rooks on the c- and d-files.
This expansion is promising. Our bishops are coming back to g2 and g3 and we'll push our kingside pawns to open up the position for them. We've also got kingside attack ideas!

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/1QP1.text:
This is the most solid, defending b7.

We'll play Nh4. Our idea is to get rid of the light-squared bishop, which is often a piece Black likes holding on to when they develop it to f5.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp3b/3P1B1N/1QP1.text:
Retreating.

With g4, we can make it flee even farther.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1BbN/1QP1P.text: Black saves the bishop for a while longer. We'll chase it with our pawns.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3PbB1N/1QP1P.text: Going towards the center. We'll push the bishop back. We would rather capture on g6 than on e4, when dxe4 would leave our h4-knight looking awkward.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pnb1/2pp4/3P1B1N/1QP1.text:
Black may want to recapture with their h-pawn to open up their rook.

We'll take anyway.
Black may have wanted to provoke f3. We'll capture.

r1q1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pnb1/2pp4/3P1BPN/1QP1.text: Now it's just back where it should've gone, and we will take it with our knight.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2pp4/Q2P1Bb1/2P1P.text:
Black blocks the pin and may think of transferring the knight to b6.

We stop that idea by adding another attacker.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1P3.text:
Bf5 is a logical possibility. Black develops their light-squared bishop. However, this move does undefend b7.

We'll develop the g1-knight.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1Bb1/2P1P3/.text: Black develops their bishop with a tempo, hitting our queen. We'll develop the g1-knight and block the threat.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
Connecting the pawns.

Now Qb3 attacks the b7-pawn and we don't mind if Black defends with their queen. 

We can use our pressure to transform the position in our favor.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1Bb1/2P1PN2.text:
Black consolidates their structure.

But we can set up a trap by pinning the c6-knight with Qa4. 

One idea is Ne5. The bonus trap is 7.Qa4 Bd6 8.Ba6! and the tactics work in our favor.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/1BbpB3/Q5b1/2P1P3/PP.text:
We recapture, opening up an attack on the bishop and attacking the g7 pawn. 

Black will lose material and we have nothing to worry about, just consolidating.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/1Bbpn3/Q4Bb1/2P1P3/P.text: If Black captures with the bishop...

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/2bp4/QP3Bb1/2PBP3/P2.text:
And we've got a great queenside initiative! 

Achieving b4 with a tempo is good for White, since b5 will follow, dislodging the knight from c6.
Further on, we have plans of Be5 to attack the g7-pawn, and 0-0. c4 is a pawn break that should be contemplated in the future.

r3kb1r/1p1n1ppp/1pn1p3/1Bpp1b2/3P1B2/2P1.text: Black has to prevent Ne5. Of course, they may just allow it if they play something natural like ...Be7.

We just castle. 

The pawns on b6 and b7 are doubled. We've got h3 ideas to preserve our strong bishop on the diagonal, and it's hard to think of a scenario in which Black will challenge our London Bishop.

Also at any point, a4 is a useful move to defend our bishop on b5.

r3kb1r/1p3ppp/1pn1pn2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
The pawns are doubled.

We'll pin the c6-knight and threaten Ne5.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qn1p3/1Bpp4/Q2P1Bb1/2P1.text:
Black defends c6.

We'll jump into e5, attacking all the knights and even the bishop on g4.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
Applying pressure on b2.

We'll grab a pawn, attacking the queen.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2Pp1b2/5B2/2P1PN2/P.text:
Grabbing our b-pawn.

We'll play Nd4, attacking bishop and knight. 

If ...Nxd4, we recapture with the c-pawn and our pawn structure is not only fixed, but extremely solid.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2nb1/2Pp4/3N1B2/2P1P3/P.text: Black retreats. We will bring our bishop out, pinning the c6-knight.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2Pp1b2/3NnB2/2P1P3/P2.text:
And we recapture. The position is fairly equal. 

We have plans of Bb5 and 0-0, but it really depends on what Black chooses to do. If they trade knights with ...Nxd2, we'll have to recapture with the king and lose castling rights. 

If ...e5, we can always capture the bishop if it's still on f5 or the knight on c6.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/2Pp1b2/3NnB2/2P1P3/Pq.text:
This move is good. It puts pressure on d2. Our queen is overloaded. It cannot defend the rook on a1 and the knight on d2 at the same time.

Thus, we'll play Qc1, offering a trade of queens.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/1BPp4/Q4Bb1/2PnP3/P.text:
Black gives this check as a distraction and as a more favorable way of returning the piece.

We've got to capture.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/1Bppn3/Q2P1Bb1/2P1P.text:
If Black gets rid of the pressure... 

This allows this jump attacking all the knights and even the bishop on g4.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/1QP1P.text:
A very popular yet inaccurate move. 

This allows us a rather forcing continuation that gives us an easier to play position. We'll begin by exchanging queens.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1BqpBb2/Q7/2P1P3/PP1.text:
Black should save their bishop.

But this allows us more attacking choices. We'll play our bishop to d4.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1Bqpn3/Q4Bb1/2P1P3/P.text: This option is just bad. We'll take on e5, uncovering an attack on the g4-bishop.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2nqp3/1B1p1b2/Q2B4/2P1P3/P.text:
The queen must go to a safe square, ideally to d6 because ...Qe7, although safe, blocks in the f8-bishop.

But we can play e4 and take advantage of the queen's position. At first sight, it looks like we're losing a pawn with this move.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2nqp3/1B1p1b2/Q2BP3/2P5/PP.text: But we can take advantage of the queen's position. It looks like we're losing a pawn with this move.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2nqp3/1B3b2/Q1NBp3/2P5/PP3.text:
This is an attack on the queen. We're practically winning. 

For example, ...Qc7, and we can castle queenside (0-0-0). We've got pressure along the d-file and Be5 is even on the horizon.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black undermines our center.

We support it with c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we'll play e3 now that the bishop is out.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We develop our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first study of this chapter! 

We're going to see what to do after black goes for the traditional d5/Nf6/c5/Nc6 setup, like we saw in Chapter 2, but this time Black will move the light-squared bishop out! 

The moves Bf5 or Bg4 will be analyzed on move 5! Let's begin with 1.d4!

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/4P3/PPP.text:
In this chapter, we will consider what happens when black plays ...Bg4 instead of Bf5.

Fortunately, our regular London move Nf3 also blocks the attack to our queen.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p3b/3P1BP1/4PN1P/.text: We'll play g4, breaking the pin.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4PQ1P/PP.text: Now we've got the bishop pair and we'll have an unopposed light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/4Pb1P/PP.text: This capture will not benefit black.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/4PN2/PP.text:
Getting ready to develop the dark-squared bishop and castle.

We will attempt to punish black's early ...Bg4 by hunting down this bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pnb1/3p4/3P1BP1/4PN1P/.text: The only way for Black to save the bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pnb1/3pN3/3P1BP1/4P2P/.text: We have an idea of playing h4-h5, trapping the g6 bishop, which is awkward to guard against. We have a nice position.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p3b/3P1B2/2N2P2/PPP.text: We can play for e4 in the future, but g4 and h4-h5 is also a serious idea when we gain time on black's bishop and threaten to trap it. This will give us a nice space advantage on the kingside.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P1Bb1/8/PPP1PPP.text:
It is also possible to play ...Bg4 on move two, but it makes less sense when it's not attacking anything yet.

We start our chase of black's bishop by playing f3. We will gain a lot of time on it and have a space advantage on the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Brings the g8 knight to the most natural square and starts developing the kingside.

We'll reinforce our d4 pawn and get ready to develop our other bishop in the future.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. This is one of Black's two most common responses.

We bring our bishop to a great square. This is the start of the London.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
This study will focus on moves we've already seen from Black at some move orders. However, not quite like this one. We're dealing with Black going d5/Nf6 and the immediate Bg4 attacking our queen. 

It's a quick study, because after we block the attack with a developing move Nf3, Black's quick excursion to the g4 square is dubious. Off we go, starting with 1.d4.

2r1k2r/1p1nbppp/p1p1pn2/2Pp1b2/1P1P1B2/2.text: We're headed to a5. We've got a whole lot more space, and we're going to attack black's weak points! Our dark-squared bishop is a nuisance in the position that cannot be traded!

2r1kb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p1pn2/2Pp1b2/1P1P1B2/.text:
Black escapes the pawn push. The rook move unpins their a-pawn.

We'll play h3, creating a square for the f4-bishop to go back to.

r1q1k2r/pp1nbppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text:
Developing the bishop.

Our knight can leap into b5!

r1q1kb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN.text: Adding another guard against the b5 jump.

r1q1kb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/3pNb2/3P1B2/1QN.text:
We jump into the center and we enjoy more space. At least we don't have a queen on c8!  

Be2 and 0-0 are next, and if ...Nxe5, we recapture with the d-pawn, removing the knight from f6. At that point, there'll be c-file pin tactics!

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3n1b2/3P1B2/1QN1.text: Recapturing with the knight is also possible.

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3n1b2/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
You can consider this a win. Black now has one less central pawn!

Rc1 and Be2 are sensible continuations. There's pressure along the c-file that Black will have to deal with.

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1Q.text:
Black defends from c8.

But our rook is ultimately coming to c1. First, we will open the c-file by capturing on d5.

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1.text:
Black takes in the center with the pawn.

With Rc1, we place the queen under immediate pressure.

r1q2rk1/pp1nbppp/2p2n2/1N1p1b2/3P1B2/1Q2.text:
Black gets out of the threatened fork on c7.

But we can still throw our bishop into d6, attacking the Black counterpart!

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppp/2pB1n2/1N1p1b2/3P4/1Q2P.text: Black defends their bishop and unpins the c-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppp/2pB1n2/1N1p1b2/3P4/Q3PN.text:
But we add another attacker! 

People will most surely take with ...Bxd6, after which Nxd6 attacks b7 and the f5-bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3n1b2/QbBP1B2/2N1P.text:
Adding pressure to c3.

We'll force black's hand by capturing on d5.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/QbPP1B2/2N1.text:
Castling.

We'll active our rook and support c3.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p1b2/Qb1P1B2/2N1PN2.text:
And castling should be better for us. Black has blocked their own c-pawn. We've got ideas of retreating the queen to pressure the b-file.

In addition, the knight can jump to a4 and later to c5.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3p1b2/QbPPnB2/2N1PN.text: Adding an attacker on the knight.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/QbPP1B2/2N1P.text:
The knight blocks the check and defends the bishop.

We proceed with development.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1p2pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text:
This move really opens up the queenside light squares a lot more, especially the entry point on b5.

Black is lost. We play Nh4 and our light square control will be brutal.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1p2pnb1/1N1p4/3P1B1N/1Q2.text:
But the absence of the c-pawn allows our knight in. 

White is winning. If ...Rc8, we first insert Nxg6 and then follow it up by taking on a7 with the knight.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1p2pnb1/3p4/3P1B1N/1QN1P.text: Trying to recapture with the h-pawn.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1pp1p3/3n1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text: Black recaptures with the knight and we will trade, eliminating the attacker of f4 prior to invading with our light-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1pp1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1QN.text:
Black pushes their pawn but this leaves weaknesses.

We can simply recapture. Our bishop gains a nice diagonal, and c6 can become tender.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/1pp2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text: Black recaptures away with the e-pawn.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/Bpp2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text: We're infiltrating. The a8-rook is in trouble.

r2qkb1r/p2n1ppp/Bpp5/3p1b2/3P1B2/1Q2PN2/.text:
And now our bishop infiltrates. 

We're already threatening Bb7 to win the exchange, which is impossible to stop.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1.text:
Black develops theirs.

We'll bring the queen out and attack the b-pawn.

r3k2r/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/2Pp1b2/3P1B2/1PN1P.text:
The idea is pure development.

But we'll push forward with the b-pawn, pressurizing the Black position!

r3kb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p1pn2/2Pp1b2/3P1B2/1PN.text:
A defense against the pawn advance to b5.

We'll still push forward.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1QN.text:
Black interposes with their queen.

We'll play c5, attacking the queen.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/2Pp1b2/3P1B2/1qN1.text:
Black trades.

We'll recapture, opening up our rook.

r4rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/2Pp1b2/1P1P1B2/2N1.text:
It was too late for a6 either way.

With b5, we now underminine the entirety of the structure and get rid of the doubled pawn.

r4rk1/pp1nbppp/4pn2/1BPp1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN2.text: And we develop the bishop with a better position. We've also got a-file doubling to come.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/2N1P3.text:
Black can elect to pin us.

But we can give a check, forcing the Black knight to block the c-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1P.text:
c6, simply defending the central pawn, is another option. 

It's ultra-solid, but the problem is the knight usually wants to go to c6. So this already is a bit passive.

We'll develop our knight.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/4P3/PP.text:
And black has developed their light-squared bishop, preparing e6.

We can begin undermining the center with c4.

The early ...Bf5 can be exploited by going for a Queen's Gambit-like approach.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/4P3/P.text:
Black supports their center.

But we bring the knight to pressure the center.

Because of c4, they'll have a hard time defending d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black brings the knight out.

We play e3 now that the bishop is out.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. 

We'll bring the bishop out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the third study of this chapter. 

We're going to see what to do against Black if they choose a setup with d5/Nf6/Bf5. 

The bishop is out of the pawn chain. However, Black chose not to put in on g4. Let's see how this is any different! We begin with 1.d4.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/P1N.text: And we get ready to expand on the queenside.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3B1b2/3P1B2/2Q1PN2.text: We can just eliminate that knight. We've got better queenside prospects than black!

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/1QN1P.text:
Black defends.

And we will castle.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/2BP1B2/1Qb1PN.text:
If Black ever captures...

We just recapture with the queen.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1P.text:
Developing the bishop.

We'll develop our king's knight.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1P.text:
Developing the knight.

We'll deploy our rook on the c-file.

r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N5/P.text:
Black can choose to develop their knight.

We'll just continue with e3.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3q1b2/3P1B2/2Q1PN2/P.text:
Black recaptures with the queen. Our queen stands better placed on the semi-open c-file! 

You don't want to take on c7 right away. Rather, just increase c-file control with a move like Rfc1. 

The knight on c6 will be glued to that square to avoid dropping c7.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
Castling.

And we attack the bishop with Qb3.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B1P/2P1P3/.text: And now we can expand with h4. We're playing Ng3 next!

rn1qk1nr/pp3ppp/2p5/3p1b2/3P1B2/2Q5/PP2P.text:
Moving the attacked pawn.

We'll shift our queen over to g3, putting pressure on the dark squares and hitting g7.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3P1b2/3P1B2/2b5/PP2.text:
Eliminating the knight might be a try.

Naturally, we will recapture.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/2N5/P.text:
Black thinks pinning us is a good idea.

But we can just capture the d-pawn.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3p1b2/1b1P1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn.

We'll attack the bishop with Qb3.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3p1b2/3P1B2/1Qb5/PP2P.text:
The bishop takes our knight.

We'll recapture with the queen, attacking c7.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P5/P3PPP.text:
Black captures with the pawn.

We'll play the calm e3.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/6Q1/PP2.text:
Developing and offering us the g-pawn.

We prefer to focus on the dark squares rather than potentially getting our queen into trouble with the black rook.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2pB1n2/3p1b2/3P4/5PQ1/PP2.text: But now f3 protects our central squares. It seems Black will have a tough time castling, too. We've also got Qe5+ ideas if Nh5 attacks our queen.

rn1qk2r/ppp2p2/3bpp1p/5b2/2BP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
Black can't recapture with the queen, as e4 and e5 wins material.

In the resulting position, we've got a better pawn structure and d5 will be played next! Dangerous stuff for Black!

rn1qk2r/ppp2pp1/3bpn1p/5bB1/2BP4/2N1P3/P.text:
Black plays h6 to attack us...

We'll capture on f6.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/5b2/2BP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
...Bd6 offering a trade is another popular move.

We'll decline. This pin comes with the tricky idea of capturing on f6.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Now pinning our knight is popular.

But we can ignore the pin and develop.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P1P3/P4.text:
Black develops.

Our knight has a good future on g3.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5b2/2pP1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
Black develops their knight.

We'll play e3, opening up our bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/2pP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Black continues with their development.

And we recover the pawn.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p1b2/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
And lo and behold! Black does the same! 

Ok! Now here we can deviate and Black can't continue copying us. With 3.c4 we're attacking the d5 pawn.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/2pP1B2/8/PP2PPPP.text:
Black can continue with this natural reaction.

We'll develop our knight.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p1b2/2PP1B2/8/PP2P.text:
Supporting the pawn with e6 is the most popular.

We'll increase the pressure in the center.

rn2k1nr/1pp2ppp/p1q1p1b1/8/3PPB2/1QP2P2/.text: And we can stop here. We've got a huge center and the bishop pair.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/2q1p1b1/8/3PPB2/1QP2P2/P.text: Threatening to win the queen with Bb5.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/2q1p1b1/8/3PPB2/2P2P2/P5.text: The queen retreats, and hits c3.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p1b1/3q4/1b1P1B2/2N2P2/.text:
Getting out of the fork.

We'll expand anyway.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p1b1/3q4/3P1B2/2P2P2/P3.text:
Stepping out of danger.

But we'll expand anyway.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3q1b2/1b1P1B2/2N5/PP.text:
Black takes with the queen because our knight is pinned.

We'll play f3. This move, threatening e4, is dangerous in many of these positions.

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3q1b2/3P1B2/2P5/P3PP.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We'll prepare to expand in the center by playing f3. We threaten a pawn fork with e4.

rn2k1nr/pppq1ppp/4p1b1/8/1b1PPB2/2N2P2/P.text:
The queen backs off.

We'll pose a question to the pinning bishop by playing a3.

rn2k1nr/pppq1ppp/4p1b1/b7/2BPPB2/P1N2P2/.text: That's ok. We'll just develop our pieces around our huge center.

rn2k1nr/pppq1ppp/4p1b1/b7/3PPB2/P1N2P2/1.text: They choose to keep the pin.

rn2k2r/ppB1qppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/3P4/6Q1/PP2P.text:
The queen moves away.

We'll attack her again. Black was trying to be tricky and get ...Qb4+ in.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. 

We get the bishop out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the study on the Copycat London. We'll deal with when Black chooses to play d5 and Bf5, essentially playing our first opening moves. 

Specifically, we're going to see setups without Nf6, because we've already got a study with d5/Nf6/Bf5 systems.

Let's get on with it, beginning with 1.d4!

lessons.title: The Noob Setup: d5, Nf6, Nc6?!

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black recaptures.

And we will develop, controlling the center.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qppp/2n1pn2/2Pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/.text:
And the queen retreats. We've got a pretty good dark-squared control. 

Attacking the c6 knight is an idea. You'll notice black's plan of e5 is harder to do since d5 lacks support.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2nqpn2/2Pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
We attack the queen and place another pawn on the dark squares.

Going for a pawn on the same color complex is a great idea after trading off the bishop of that color complex.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/2n1pn1p/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1.text: Black creates luft for their king.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/2n1pn1p/3p4/2PP1B2/P1N.text:
And we get ready to play on the queenside, where Black is clumsy because of the c6-knight blocking the c-pawn. 

With our rook coming to the c-file, we'll have a scenario in which there'll be some x-raying pressure on c7. 

We'll want to delay the light-squared bishop development to give Black some time to play ...dxc4 to let us recapture with the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1P.text:
They castle.

We'll give our bishop gets a retreat square. 

If Black goes for ...Be7, there's no reason why we shouldn't aim to keep our dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal unopposed.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/1bPP1B2/2N1P.text:
And we develop our knight. We've got plans of Bd3 and castling kingside. 

Black might continue with Ne4, but the knight on c3 is sufficiently defended. 

If there are trades on c3, this would only give us another c-pawn that we can use to undermine the Black center.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1P3.text:
Developing the bishop is also an option. 

However, it does nothing for the situation in the center.

We'll develop our knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/1bPP1B2/2N1P3.text:
Black can choose to pin us. 

We'll protect our knight by bringing our rook to c1.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
This move is also quite popular, proposing a trade of bishops.

We'll accept, because we believe we have the better light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PP.text:
And Black gets the other knight out. 

We undermine the center with c4! With Black's c-pawn immobile, undermining d5 becomes a whole lot more effective. That's why we're going for c4 instead of the usual London-style setup.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/4P3/P.text:
Black supports their central strongpoint.

We'll develop our knight, pressurizing d5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black blocks their c-pawn. 

We'll play our standard e3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. 

We'll enter the London!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to another chapter on the London! 

Many players, I bet, will bring their knight out on c6, blocking their c-pawn. 

This is one of the three studies in which we'll explore moves after black does this. In this case, we'll see the setup after Black gets both knights out after ...d5.

We begin with 1.d4!

lessons.title: Reverse Jobava London: d5, Nc6, Bf5

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
The knight is developed.

We'll support our center with e3.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1PN.text:
And now our rook enters the party on the c-file! 

Black has accomplished nothing out of the opening and all our pieces are properly placed. Meanwhile there's a Black knight on c6 which doesn't have any prospects. Qe2 or Qb3 are good ideas to develop the queen, followed by Rfd1.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/2N1P.text:
Now a popular move for Black is to pin our knight.

We'll capture on d5.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
Bb4 pinning our knight is now a very common move.

But we can develop our king's knight on e2, where it protects our other knight. The pin is ineffective.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p1b2/1b1P1B2/2N1P3/.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll bring our other knight out to defend c3. We also have Ng3 ideas.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n1bn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1NBP1N.text:
And we bring our bishop out to a safe d3 square where it controls the light squares leading to h7. 

b4, then b5 is useful in these setups.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n1pn2/3p1bB1/2PP4/P1N1P.text:
Black blocks the pin and thus improves their defense of d5.

We'll exchange minor pieces on f6.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/P1N1P3.text: They retreat. Now we'll attack the other bishop with Ng3.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pb2/3p1b2/2PP4/P1N1P3/.text:
Black recaptures.

Now we'll force Black's bishop away. We're going to fianchetto and pressure the weak d5 point.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1P3/.text: Black brings out their final minor piece.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
People seem to love this pin for some reason.

But we can just ignore it and castle.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/1bBP1B2/P1N1P3.text:
Black's ...Bb4 operation only served to give us more time and development and to start our queenside play with a tempo. 

We'll play b4, Rc1 and 0-0 next, with constant threats of b5 to force the knight off the c6-square.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2bb1/3p4/3P2P1/P1N1P3/1.text:
And we have developed with tempi and are putting pressure on the black position! 

Qb3 is on the way, attacking b7 and d5 at the same time.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/1b1P1B2/2N1P3.text: Black develops. We'll attack the bishop on b4 by playing a3.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/P1N1P.text:
Black could, for example, continue with ...Bd6.

But we'll pin the defender of d5.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/4P3/.text:
Nf6 is another way of supporting d5.

We'll develop our knight, pressurizing d5.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/1nPP1B2/2N1P3.text:
But we can simply defend c2 with our rook, with a3 to come.

After a3, we still have b4 ideas and we'll continue with our kingside development.
This was one of the ideas of Nc6 and Bf5.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1P.text:
Black supports their center.

We'll prevent the bishop from coming to b4.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5b2/2BP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
This sound developing move is also played.

We'll also develop.

r2qkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p1b2/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
And Black plays their bishop out where it eyes our c2 pawn. 

Let's not fall for ...Nb4 ideas.

With c4, we undermine the center! This move is more effective when d5 lacks support. That's why we go for it right away, instead of our usual c3/d4/e3 structure.

r2qkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/5b2/2pP1B2/4P3/PP3P.text:
Taking is another popular reaction. This lessens Black's central control.

We'll recapture with the bishop, improving our development.

r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3p1b2/2PP1B2/4P3/P.text:
...e6 supports the central pawn.

We'll develop our queen's knight. 5...Nf6 would be a transposition to the 4...Nf6 line.

r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/5b2/2BP1B2/4P3/PP3.text:
Blocking our bishop's view of f7.

We'll develop yet another piece. Our control of e4 is greater now that the pawn isn't on d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black responds in like manner.

We'll get our bishop out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study Black will combine the idea of bringing the knight out to c6 early, and bringing the bishop out to f5. 

When this happens, we can undermine the center with c4. Let's  begin with 1.d4 and see what happens!

r1bqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/2n2p2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PP.text:
And now f6. The direct idea is e5.

Achieving this for black would liberate their position and would justify f6. 

We'll play Bd3, which controls the g6 square and threatens Qh5+, when the black king may lose castling rights or, if they block with g6, we take with the bishop on d3!

r1bqkbnr/ppp1p2p/2n2pp1/3p4/3P1B2/3BP3/P.text:
g6 removes the possibility of checking Black on the h5 square.

Let's just develop normally and control the square that Black wanted to expand on.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black develops the knight.

We play our natural developing move, connecting our pawns and getting ready to develop our light-squared bishop.

r2qk1nr/ppp2bpp/2nbpp2/3p4/3P4/3BPNB1/PP.text:
Proposing a bishop trade.

We'll push c4 and undermine d5!

r2qk2r/ppp1nbpp/2nbpp2/3p4/2PP4/2NBPNB1/.text:
But we can continue adding pressure.

It seems Black's development with f6/Be6/Bf7 has left them with an ineffective setup. 

We can add pressure with a3 and b4 and with Qc2.

r2qk2r/ppp1nbpp/2nbpp2/3p4/2PP4/3BPNB1/P.text: The knight helps support the center.

r2qkbnr/1pp1p2p/p1n2pp1/1B1p4/3P1Bb1/4PN.text:
Black tries to pressure us into giving up the bishop pair.

We'll accept, as this makes e7-e5 harder.

r2qkbnr/2p1p2p/p1p2pp1/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN.text:
In terms of opening advantage, we've got it, as we've effectively prevented e5 and thus f6 seems odd. 

Our king will be safer on the kingside, and we can even go Re1 and e4 later to open up the position in our favor.

r2qkbnr/2p1p2p/p1p2pp1/3p4/3P1Bb1/4PN2/P.text:
Recapturing.

Now we get rid of the pin. If Black gives us the bishop for the knight, then it's a plus. They no longer have the bishop pair advantage. 

If Black moves away, we unpin our knight and thus control e5 sufficiently.

r2qkbnr/ppp1p1pp/2n1bp2/3p4/3P1B2/3BP3/P.text:
This is the top engine move. It is popular enough that we should consider it. It counters our check on h5 because the bishop would be able to block it with ...Bf7.

We'll develop, controlling e5.

r2qkbnr/ppp1p2p/2n2p2/1B1p2p1/3P1Bb1/4PN.text:
Attacking our bishop.

We'll go to the only safe square.

r2qkbnr/ppp1p2p/2n2pp1/3p4/3P1Bb1/3BPN2/.text:
Black pins us, effectively gaining control of e5 for a potential pawn break next move. How do we lessen Black's control of e5?

We create a pin of our own! The knight no longer supports ...e7-e5.

r2qkbnr/ppp1p3/2n2p2/1B1p1bpp/2PP4/4PNBP.text: Now we can undermine the center. Black isn't ready for the position to open up against them.

r2qkbnr/ppp1p3/2n2p2/1B1p2pp/3P2b1/4PNB1.text:
Threatening to trap our bishop.

We'll play h3 and create an escape square while attacking the g4-bishop. Remember, if 8...Bxf3, we benefit from taking one of Black's only developed pieces.

r2qkbnr/ppp1pbpp/2n2p2/3p4/3P1B2/3BPN2/P.text:
Black relocates the bishop, with the potential to move the e-pawn. Moves like 5...Qd7, could be met with 6. Nc3, and our threat of Nb5 looms over the position.

We'll preempt a potential g5, and retreat the bishop.

r2qkbnr/ppp2bpp/2n1pp2/3p4/3P4/3BPNB1/PP.text:
...e6 supporting the center could be played. ...e5 is impossible.

We'll castle.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We develop our bishop as before.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the last study of the early Nc6 chapter. 

Black's idea for this one is simple: play ...f6 and achieve an early e5 or g5 break. Of course, we'll do our best to prevent this pawn break by threatening a lethal tactic at the beginning that many people fall for!

Let's get the game underway with our queen's pawn!

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
And we create a retreat square for our bishop. 

As you can see, h3 also takes a square away from Black's bishop, and they have to find a way to develop that piece in the current structure. Meanwhile we'll develop with Nbd2 and our rooks coming to the central files.
Black develops to pressure the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp2n1pp/2n1pp2/8/2BP1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
And we defend it! We can agree that e6 is awkward for Black: it blocks their light-squared bishop. 

We can castle kingside and play Re1, but d5 is also a great move that can destabilize Black's position quickly if they're not careful. 

d5 and with the bishop on c4 piercing through the diagonal, it'll even be hard for the king to find a safe space.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN.text: And we continue developing, bearing in mind the fact that perhaps Black is delaying the capture on c4 until we develop our f1 bishop. We've got, in the meantime, useful moves to play like h3 and Rc1.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp4/3P1B2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black tries to liberate their position and get some counterplay.

We stay solid and support our center with c3.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PNB1/.text:
And our development continues normally, with Bd3 and e4 to come! 

After 0-0, we'll bring rooks to d1 and e1 to support our central expansion.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/PP.text:
Black castles.

And we castle too.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Achieving their fianchetto.

We'll develop and control e5.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
Preparing to castle.

Let's develop and control the center.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Offering a trade of Black's good bishop.
 
We would prefer to exchange on our terms, and not bring the Black queen into the center. Our bishop steps back.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
Black gets ready to castle.

We get ready to put our king into safety.

Notice we bring our bishop out to e2 whenever there's a pawn on g6. The bishop's scope isn't as good on d3 when the g6-pawn blocks its influence.

rnbqkb1r/pp2n1pp/4pp2/2p5/2pP1B2/2NBP3/P.text:
Capturing away from the center.

We'll recapture with the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2n1pp/4pp2/2pp4/2PP1B2/3BP3/P.text:
Black chooses to do the same, but this setup with ...f6 is unnatural. 

The dark-squared bishop is stuck behind the knight.

Here we just develop. The idea is that any capture in the center isn't going to solve black's problems or improve their position.

rnbqkb1r/pp2n1pp/4pp2/8/2Bp1B2/2N1P3/PP3.text:
Another central pawn exchange.

With our lead in development, we embrace the isolated queen's pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Now Black develops the knight.

Let's undermine their d5 pawn. 

Our standard development of c4/Nc3 will be effective if Black blocks in their light-squared bishop with e6 at some point.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/4P3/PP.text: Black will often defend their center. We'll develop our queen's knight, and target d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1n1pp/4pp2/3p4/3P1B2/3BP3/PP.text:
The knight adds a defender to the g6 square.

Undermining the center is good, plus Black has developed suboptimally, therefore opening the position is to our advantage.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPP.text:
And Black plays this passive move, which usually ends up with the bishop behind the pawn. 

We will support our center, as before, with e3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/5p2/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black opens up their king early. Perhaps they intend e5?

e3 is good and if 3...Nc6, we'll transpose to something familiar.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
The idea is to fianchetto the bishop. It's not particularly ambitious, though.

Let's continue with our standard developing move.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us. 

We'll continue with our standard strategy and play Bf4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/4pp2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2P.text:
This is a non-losing move that deviates from the d5/Nc6/f6 positions we already know.

But here we can still threaten the check on h5!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
This chapter will prove useful if you play against any noobs who play 1...d5 and then play a random second move that we haven't seen thus far. 

You'll notice many things can transpose, especially in 2...c6 and 2...f6. 

We'll begin with 1.d4.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/1pn1p3/1N1n4/Q4B2/4PN2/.text:
Our queen can just sidestep the threat and still defend f4. Meanwhile, we're landing something on d6 quite soon.

0-0-0 will also be a powerful move that places a rook on the d-file and pressurizes Black.

r2qkb1r/5ppp/ppnpbn2/2p3N1/5B2/2N1P3/PPP.text:
Black could desperately seek to continue to develop. 

If they go back, they just lose a tempo. 

We'll take on e6.

r2qkb1r/6pp/ppnppn2/2p5/5BP1/2N1P3/PPP2P.text:
And now that the light squares are ours, we can have a party on them! 

With Bg2, we'll control the long diagonal, specially considering that the light-squared bishop isn't on the board. 

g5 also threatens to remove the knight from f6: it's hard to suggest a move for Black.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/np2p3/1N6/2NpnB2/4P3/PP.text:
Now the knight must jump forward to defend d6.

But after exd4, our knights are well placed in the queenside and we have good development. 

Meanwhile Black has been forced into odd contortions to defend themselves.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/np2pn2/1N6/3p1B2/4P3/PP.text:
Supposing Black thinks they're off the hook in the center...

We'll make them think again with Nc4, focusing on the d6 square.
