We'll continue with our plan.

r1bqkr2/pp1nppQp/2p3p1/4n1N1/2B5/2N5/PPP.text:
...Nge5 defends f7 again, but that means it must stay on e5.

We play a bold temporary sacrifice on d7. The point is to eliminate the defender of the f8-rook.

r1bqkr2/pp1nppQp/2p3p1/8/2B3n1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
The rook must defend f7.

But our knight jumps into the fray, hitting f7 and h7.

r1r3k1/p2np1bp/b2p1npB/q1p5/1p1PP1P1/5P2.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll remove the defensive bishop by exchanging on g7, after which our queen will have access to h6.

r1r3k1/p2np2p/b2p1npQ/q1p5/1p1PPNP1/5P2/.text: And just as an example of how to end a game in the Pirc, we activate yet another piece. Black will have to relinquish material in order to avoid mate.

r1r3k1/p2nppbp/b2p1npB/q1p4P/1p1PP1P1/5P.text:
Black, under great pressure, tries to activate more pieces. Moving the f-rook also gives the king extra room...

But our attack is too quick: we open the h-file by capturing on g6.

r1r5/p2np1kp/b2p1np1/q1p5/1p1PP1P1/5P2/P.text:
Once the king recaptures...

We've got Qh6+ and we're breaking through!

r2qkr2/pp1bppQN/2p3p1/4n3/2B5/2N5/PPP2P1.text:
We capture on h7 and threaten to take on f8 with checkmate. 

Black is lost.

r2qkr2/pp1bppQp/2p3p1/4n1N1/2B5/2N5/PPP2.text: So after either the bishop or the queen recapture...

r4rk1/p2nppbp/b1pp1npB/q7/1p1PP2P/5P2/PP.text:
After something like ...Ba6 with the idea of activating the bishop...

g4 is way too strong: it allows us to play h5 at some point.

r4rk1/p2nppbp/b2p1npB/q1p5/1p1PP1PP/5P2/.text:
This counter-attack is too slow.

We'll push ahead with h5.

rnb1k2r/p3pp1p/2pp1np1/7q/1p1PP3/3B1N2/P.text:
Take a look at this position. Whose pieces look better? Black has clearly gone astray.

e5 is a strong pawn break that's sufficiently supported by our knight on f3.

rnb1k2r/p3pp1p/2pp1npQ/7q/1p1PP3/3B1N2/P.text:
Black could beg for a queen trade.

They may try going for this because our queen is preventing them from castling.

rnb1k2r/p3pp1p/2pp1npQ/q7/1p1PP3/2NB1N2/.text:
...b4 attacks our knight. But our position is solid. 

We can just move the knight away and nothing bad happens.

We come back to e2, and,as the bishop isn't on f1 anymore, our knight doesn't block it.

rnb1k2r/p3pp1p/2pp1npQ/qp6/3PP3/2NB4/PPP.text: After ...b5, our pieces are simply too well placed.

rnb1k2r/pp2pp1p/2pp1npQ/q7/3PP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Our knight is pinned, so ...Nxe4 is a threat.

We defend e4 with the bishop and develop another piece.

rnbq1rk1/p3ppbp/2pp1npB/1p6/3PP3/2N5/PPP.text:
Black attacks on the queenside.

Our next move, f3, safeguards the e4 pawn and guards the g4 square.

It removes much of the force behind ...b4 since our center is protected.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Preparing the usual counterplay.

We'll offer a trade of bishops by playing Bh6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Castling is by far the most popular move here.

We'll continue with our plan.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/6p1/4Pp1n/3P1P2/2N5/PP.text:
We are in complete control of Black's kingside. The knight is dim on the rim, and the bishop stares at a wall of pawns. 

We'll develop with g3 and Bg2, Be3 to get the dark-squared bishop out.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/6p1/4Pp1n/3P4/2N5/PPP2.text: When will the knight see the light of day again?

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Believe it or not, thousands of people have played this. The idea is developing the entire kingside and ask questions later. I'm afraid chess doesn't work that way though; you must pay attention to your opponent's threats as well.

We'll push e5, displacing the knight!

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/6p1/4P2n/3P1B2/2N5/PPP.text: This doesn't place the knight on the back rank. It attacks our bishop, but when we retreat, we are then threatening to win the knight with g4!

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2p2npQ/1p2p3/3P4/2N5/PPP2.text:
Black may try to trade once.

But this recapture opens up the d-file. 

When you don't have a good reason to trade, you shouldn't. And this applies for Black here.

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2p3pQ/1p1nP3/8/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
So we can pin it to the queen! 

We've got serious pressure against the knight on d5, and we're threatening just to win a pawn after Nxd5. If ...e6, there's Ne4 intending Nf6+ or Nd6+.

The position isn't easy to play for Black, as some quick analysis will show.
The knight goes on the open d-file.

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2pp1npQ/1p6/3PP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Starting the queenside attack! 

Black often plays this move to initiate their counterplay and some pressure against a2.

We'll push forward with e5, and dislodge the knight.

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2pp1npQ/4P3/1p1P4/2N5/PPP.text:
A counter-attack. Perhaps not a good idea.

We can just go back and defend our d4-pawn. The knight on f6 is still under attack.

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2pp2pQ/3nP3/1p1P4/5N2/PPP.text:
And we've got some pretty dangerous pieces. 

Meanwhile Black has to deal with our kingside initiative. Because our knight on e2 blocks the bishop, we can fianchetto with g3 and Bg2 followed by 0-0.

rnbqk2r/p3pp1p/2pp2pQ/3nP3/1p1P4/8/PPP1N.text: The knight goes to the center of the board.

rnbqk2r/pp2pp1p/2pp1npb/8/3PP3/2N5/PPPQ1.text:
Black accepts the trade.

And we recapture. 

Our queen is now an invader in the dark squares.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPPQ.text:
A standard move in this position. The idea is to control some central squares, delay castling, and prepare ...b5.

Let's trade bishops! This gets rid of an important defender of the dark squares and allows our queen an entry point.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPP2.text:
This is officially Pirc territory. Don't worry, we've got a plan for this too.

The plan is basically: trade bishops, get the queen to the h-file, trade h-pawns and open up the rook, and give mate on the h-file. Sounds easy, doesn't it? Sometimes it is.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1PP.text:
Black fianchettoes. This is very natural, as this was the objective of ...g6. 

And we'll play e4! One of the benefits of Nc3: it supports the e2-e4 push!

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1P.text: Here I recommend the immediate Nc3. I know it blocks our c-pawn. However, we're able to influence the center quicker.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Alright, now here Black starts to deviate from what we know. 

It seems they want to fianchetto. Indeed, this is what happens in the Grunfeld and King's Indian! 

Here I recommend the immediate Nc3. I know it blocks our c-pawn. However, we're able to influence the center quicker.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black plays their standard Nf6. 

Let's bring the bishop out. This is the London!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to another chapter on 1...Nf6 from Black. This time, we'll explore lines that have to do with a Nf6/g6 setup from Black: usually, the black player will intend to play Grunfeld or King's Indian positions.

We'll see that in this study, we'll be able to drift play into Pirc territory, and there our game plan will be quite simple: attack! Let's begin with 1.d4.

rnbqnrk1/ppppppbp/6p1/4P3/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1.text:
The point is to castle long and attack on the kingside.

h4 and h5 to attack the hook on g6 and open up the h-file for the rook.

rnbqnrk1/ppppppbp/6p1/4P3/3P1B2/2N5/PPP2.text: I don't think I've seen a worse knight this early on. It looks like a 960 position.

2r2rk1/pp1bp1bp/5np1/q2p4/3P1BP1/2NB1P2/.text:
We've got many pieces facing the kingside, and our attack will consequently be strong.

The queen could stay on d2 to defend. Kb1 is a key defensive move, while Rde1 goes on the offensive to attack e7.

2r2rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/q2p1b2/3P1B2/2N2P2/P.text:
The rook enters the semi-open c-file.

But we'll begin our attack with g4.

r1b2r2/pp3pk1/2n2np1/q1ppp3/3P3R/2N1P3/P.text:
A blunder like this just allows us to accelerate e4...

Firstly we exchange pawns on e5.

r1b2r2/pp3pk1/5np1/q1ppn3/4P2R/2N5/PPPQN.text:
And we're either winning a pawn in the center or entering h6 with our queen.

White is better.

r1b2rk1/p3ppb1/2p2np1/q1Pp3p/5B1P/2N1P3/.text:
Recapturing.

And after we play a3...

r1b2rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/q1PpN2p/5B1P/2N1P.text:
Should they try to regain the pawn with the queen...

We'll take on c6.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/q1pp4/3P1B2/2N1P3.text:
The queen usually comes out to a5 to put pressure on the a2-pawn and to get out of the d-file because the rook is coming to the file.

We'll play Bh6. The idea is to trade an important defender.

r1b2rk1/pp3p2/2n2npR/q1ppp3/3P4/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black may choose to undermine our center...

But the rook falls back to h4, defending the center, while secretly clearing the h6 square for the queen. So you can imagine that after e4 at some point, the queen will be able to land on h6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2p1bp/2n2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2N1P3.text:
Putting pressure on our center.

We'll reply with Nf3, supporting our center.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2N1P3.text:
Black may develop the knight, putting pressure on d4.

We'll develop ours as well.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/2n2np1/2ppN2p/3P1B1P/2N.text:
Black continues to put pressure in our center.

But here I advise taking on c5. Black has a funny way to go wrong.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppb1/n4np1/1Npp3p/3P1B1P/2P1.text:
Black castles.

Let's just develop. Black is paralyzed on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/n4np1/1Npp4/3P1B1P/4PN2.text:
Black castles.

And we continue our development. Practically we argue that our pieces are better than Black's because of the a6 knight and the c8 bishop that hasn't found a square yet.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppbp/8/3p3Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/PPP.text: The best defensive resource, planning to bring the knight to f6.

r1bq1rk1/pppnppbp/8/3p3Q/3P1B2/2NBP3/PPP.text:
Yet we're adding many attackers. We have great compensation for the exchange!

We'll play Nf3, 0-0-0, and Rh1 at some point to attack the h7-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppb1/n4np1/1Npp3p/3P1B1P/4PN2.text:
The knight has to go to the rim in order to defend c7.

We'll consolidate our center with c3.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/n4np1/1Npp4/3P1B1P/4P3/P.text:
Defending c7 from an awkward square.

We'll continue by developing another piece.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppb1/n4np1/1N1p3p/P1pP1B1P/2.text:
And after c4, disconnecting our bishop from our knight...

The simple b3 undermines Black's pawn chain.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppb1/n4np1/1N1p3p/P2P1B1P/1p.text:
What else? Black was losing material otherwise...

We now recapture with the queen. The paralyzed queenside is now within our aim.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppb1/n4np1/1Npp3p/3P1B1P/2P1.text:
Attacking our knight.

We just support it with the a-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/n4np1/1N1p4/P1pP1B1P/4P.text:
Disconnecting our knight and bishop.

But we can centralize the knight and attack the bishop on d7.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/n4np1/1Npp4/3P1B1P/4PN2.text:
Black places the bishop on d7.

We'll support the knight with our pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp2p1bp/2n2np1/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2N1P.text:
If Bf5 trying to develop another minor piece...

We can take on c5.

r2q1rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/1n1p4/2NP1B2/4P3/1P.text:
We're capturing on c4 with check and getting the piece back if Black takes our knight with the d5-pawn. 

We'll be a pawn up with a better position.

r2q1rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/1n1pN3/2pP1B2/4P3/1.text: Black captures away from the center and leaves a pawn on h7.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/1n1pN3/2pP1B2/2P1P3.text: And we've got a plan: Qc2 and taking on g6, opening up everything on the kingside!

r2q1rk1/pp2ppb1/n1b2np1/1N1p3p/P2P1B1P/1.text: Bc6 would be a good defensive move, guarding all the weak points.
But after castling, we've got plans of Rc1 and c4, and stand better.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/1n1pN2P/2pP1B2/4P3/.text:
Black takes on b5.

And we'll open up the h-file!

r2q1rk1/ppn1ppbp/5np1/1P1pN3/2pP1B1P/4P3.text:
Black attacks b5.

We'll push forward on the kingside, supported by our bishop.

Yes, we're giving up the b5-pawn, but the attack is worth it.

r2qk2r/1p1n1pb1/p1p1pnp1/3p3p/3PPB1P/2N2.text:
Black prepares a queenside pawn storm.

We'll put our rook on the semi-open g-file.

r2qk2r/pp1n1pb1/2p1pnp1/3p3p/3PPB1P/2N2P.text:
Black sets up a triangle pawn formation.

We'll take the precaution of removing our king from the queen's diagonal.

r2qk2r/pp1nppb1/2p2np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PP.text:
Developing the knight...

We'll break in the center with e4.

r2qk2r/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/3p4/3P1BbP/2N1PN2.text:
Black develops the knight.

And we'll get our knight into the center and attack the bishop.

r2qk2r/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/3pN3/3P1B1P/2N1P3.text:
And our queen is left on the e-file where it will support f3/g4 pawn pushes. 

We're also castling queenside! With our rooks coming to the kingside, we'll be trying to open up this side of the board to attack.

r3k2r/1p1n1pb1/p1p1pnp1/3p2Bp/1q1PP2P/2N.text: It seems to me all our pieces are developed, our bishops are putting a lot of pressure on the position, and Black has nothing in terms of an attack.
Should Black try to get out of the pin and place their queen actively...

r3k2r/1p1nqpb1/p1p1pnp1/3p3p/3PPB1P/2N2P.text:
Black develops the queen...

But we can immediately exploit the queen's position.

r4rk1/pp2p1bp/2n2np1/2qp1b2/3N1B2/2N1P3/.text:
Supposing the queen just takes...

We'll castle queenside and just proceed with our plan.

r4rk1/pp2p1bp/2n2np1/q1Pp1b2/5B2/2N1PN2/.text:
Black obviously will try to recover it.

But our knight aggressively jumps into the center.

If ...Nxd4, we recapture with the pawn and reinforce c5.

r4rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/2qp1b2/3n1B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
Should Black think our knight is too annoying on d4...

We can recapture with the pawn, and conveniently form a queen and bishop battery!

r4rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/q2p1b2/3P1B2/2N5/PPPQ.text:
Getting out of the way and pressurizing a2.

But f3 controls the central squares.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppb1/2p2np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PP.text:
Supporting d5.

But now we castle queenside and after e4 we'll have a queen and bishop battery!

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/3P1BbP/2N1PN2.text:
Should the knight be pinned...

We simply unpin by bringing the bishop to e2.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1BbP/2N1PN2.text: Black pins our knight, but we're not worried about our pawns being doubled..

rnbq1rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Black opens up the f-file for their rook.

We'll play Qd2 in accordance with our plan.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Capturing towards the center.

Our rook has become active on the h-file.

Our queen clears the way for castling. We'll have some central pressure, as well as the possibility of connecting rooks.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppb1/5np1/2ppN2p/3P1B1P/2N1P.text:
Black begins immediate counterplay against our center.

We'll play Qd2 to castle queenside.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp3P/3P1B2/2N1P3/.text:
Black goes for counterplay in the center!

We'll capture and open the h-file.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN.text:
Castling is the most popular move. It's a useful developing move and places the king in a safer square.

We'll bring our knight to the outpost on e5!

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.text:
Black castles. It seems they are not afraid of our h-pawn.

But we'll push it forward!

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3p3n/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
The knight just takes...

We'll sacrifice the exchange to ruin the pawn cover around the black king.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/8/3p3p/3P1B2/2N1P3/PPP.text:
Recapturing. What else?

Our queen will take on h5 and enter the attack.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppb1/5np1/2pp3p/3P1B1P/2N1PN2.text:
c5 undermines the center.

But this allows us to threaten c7 check.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.text:
Black can continue with slower play. 

The problem with this is that they take away c6 from the knight.

Let's just develop normally.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp4/3P1B1P/2N1P3/P.text:
Immediately undermining the center.

We now play Nb5, threatening Nc7. Although we don't often to play it, it makes Black develop in an awkward way with Na6.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppb1/5np1/3p3p/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.text:
h5 is the most popular move, therefore we will start here. The idea is to stop our pawn advance.

We'll just develop another piece.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black fianchettoes.

And we can begin launching our kingside attack!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PPP.text:
And Black now covers the e4 square with ...d5, and they've entered a Grunfeld setup. 

We can't play e4, so instead we'll support our center with e3.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Black will fianchetto.

Now, seeing how those Pirc positions were so good for us, let's try aiming for that again. We play Nc3.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black begins, intending a hyper-modern approach.

Our bishop comes out in standard London fashion.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
So we've already seen positions with Nf6/g6. However, in the previous study, Black didn't move any central pawns and basically allowed us to transpose into a Pirc. 

In this study, Black will play ...g6 and ...d5, preventing us from going e4. We can call this the Grunfeld Setup. Let's begin with our traditional 1.d4.

1r1q1rk1/1pnnppbp/p2p2p1/2pP4/P3PB2/2NQ1.text:
If Black tries to force the expansion...

We cover the b5 push and can respond with en passant, damaging Black's structure.

1r1q1rk1/2nnppbp/p2p2p1/PppP4/4PB2/2NQ1N.text: Just to illustrate, ...b5 wouldn't be a good idea because we can capture en passant.

3q1rk1/2nnppbp/pr1p2p1/2pP4/4PB2/3Q1N2/1.text:
We bring the knight back. We've got plans of mounting pressure on the a-pawn. 

c3 will block off the bishop's diagonal. Nd2-Nc4 may be a plan at the right moment.

r1bq1r1k/pp1nbpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/P3P2P/2N5/.text:
But our pawn storm begins, supported by our bishop! 

h5 is coming, and once we open up the h-file we'll take the knight on g7 forcing the king to recapture. We'll then begin transferring pieces to the kingside to attack the king.

r1bq1r1k/pp1nbpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/P3P3/2N5/1.text: The king tries to make room for other pieces. Note how cramped Black is.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nppbp/p2p1np1/1BpP4/P3PB2/2N.text: Black forces our bishop to retreat.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nppbp/p2p1np1/2pP4/P3PB2/2N2.text:
We keep all our pieces on the board and black is cramped. 

We'll continue with 0-0, Qd2, h3 to keep pieces out of g4 and our position is solid with more space.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/P3P3/2N2N2.text:
Black blocks, however this implies that there will be a pin on g7. 

It's not a good sign to have a fianchettoed knight.

We decide to maneuver with the f3-knight. The idea is to support h4-h5 with the bishop's influence.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpp1/3p1n1p/1BpPp3/P3P3/2N5.text:
Black castles.

And we'll develop our other knight and get ready to castle.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/4P3/2N5/PP.text:
Black develops their knight.

We will also develop our knight. Our pieces are less cramped. 

After ...Nbd7, ...Bg4 isn't a threat so we can bring our knight out.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/P3PB2/2N5.text:
Black castles.

We'll develop our knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n1p/1BpPp3/4P3/2N5/P.text:
Black prefers to leave the bishops on.

Now a4 is a useful move, expanding on the queenside.

r1bqk2r/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/4PB2/2N5/P.text:
Black blocks with the knight. This leaves their minor pieces somewhat uncoordinated.

We will play a4, working to make it harder for Black to expand on the queenside with ...a6 and ...b5.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbp1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/P3P3/2N2N2.text:
Black's lack of squares for their pieces forces them to create a weakness in the kingside.

We attack the rook with our bishop.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbpp1/3p3p/1BpPp3/P3P3/2N3N1.text:
Our knight can be transferred to g3 where it has a future on f5. In this position, we have great control over both sides of the board because of our center.

We can imagine a future with the bishop back to e2 after something like a6 attacking it, and a kingside pawn storm from us!

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbpp1/3p3p/1BpPp3/P3P3/2N5/1.text: If Black seeks to prepare kingside counterplay...

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbppp/3p4/2pPp3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black may try to go for a pawn break by inserting the ...Ne8 maneuver.

But we can just continue expanding and play a4. Notice how castling isn't a priority at the moment. 

The center is so closed that we can just continue making minor improvements.

r2k1b1r/1p1n1ppp/p3bn2/2p1B3/8/2N5/PPP2P.text:
And we pin the knight to the king. Our coordination is superior in this queenless middle game. 

When the king leaves the d-file, we can go Bg3 and then develop with Nh3, aiming at the f4-square.

r2q1rk1/1pnnppbp/p2p2p1/2pP4/P3PB2/2N2N2.text:
The idea is b5.

So we'll cover the expansion with our queen.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/n2p1np1/1BpP4/P3PB2/2N2.text:
Black develops their knight to the only available square.

We'll castle, finishing our development.

r2q1rk1/ppnbppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/P3PB2/2N2N.text:
Rerouting the knight and attacking our bishop. 

We trade off our worst piece.

r2q1rk1/ppnnppbp/3p2p1/2pP4/P3PB2/2N2N2/.text:
Black recaptures with the knight.

We'll play Re1, preparing a future e5.

rn1k1b1r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/2p1p3/5B2/2N5/PPP2.text: The king recaptures, but loses castling rights. We'll simply take on e5.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/P3PB2/2N5.text:
Black castles.

We'll develop our knight.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/4PB2/2N5/P.text:
Black blocks with the bishop and proposes a trade.

a4 is a useful move to control the queenside, and the trade isn't bad for us.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p2pbn2/2p5/4PB2/2N5/PPP2.text:
The bishop recaptures.

We will push e5, attacking the knight and the pawn.

The idea is that we're forcing a pawn trade, exposing the queens along the d-file, which will lead to a trade that's favorable for us.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/2p1p3/5B2/2N5/PPP2.text: When Black takes our pawn, we can misplace their king by exchanging queens.

rn1qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/4p3/1ppP3n/8/5P1N/PPP1.text:
Attacking d5.

We'll play e4, supporting our d-pawn.

rn2kb1r/pb1p1ppp/1q2p3/1ppP3n/2P1P3/5P1N.text:
And c4 should consolidate our center.

We can expand on the kingside with g4 and face virtually no adverse consequences on the dark squares. 

Nc3 and Bxc4 if Black takes on c4 are some moves to develop, with 0-0 coming up next.

rn2kb1r/pb1p1ppp/4p3/qppP3n/4P3/5P1N/PPP.text:
If this check ever comes...

We'll just block it with our bishop and attack the queen.

rnb1k2r/pp2bpp1/1q1p1n1p/2pPp1B1/4P3/2N5.text:
Wanting to get rid of the bishop...

Merely retreating is good.

rnb1k2r/pp2bppp/1q1p1n2/2pPp1B1/8/2N5/PP.text:
Developing and defending.

We'll build a strong center with e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/1q2p3/2pP4/4nB2/2N5/PP.text:
Simply taking the pawn that looked free, with the idea of Qb4+, is a possibility as well.

We'll capture on e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/1q2pn2/2pP4/5B2/2N5/PP.text:
Undermining the pawn with e6 is another alternative. 

We'll support our center with e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2pP4/1q2NB2/8/PPP2.text:
This move forks our pieces. 

However, there's a way to deal with this which involves giving the knight back. We'll start with Qd2.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2pP4/4qB2/8/PPPQ1P.text:
Black takes with check.

We'll block with the knight, developing yet another piece. 

So we have bishop, queen and knight developed whereas Black only has their queen out.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2pq4/5B2/8/PPPQNPP.text:
Black grabs another pawn. 

But we're so far ahead in development that we can exchange queens and then go on the attack!

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2pP4/4PB2/2N5/PqP.text:
This accelerates our development. The black queen is badly misplaced.

We've got Nb5 ideas to threaten a check on c7.
The queen could take on b2, attacking the knight.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2p5/3p1B2/2N5/PPP2PP.text: If Black tries to hold on to it...

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2pN4/3p1B2/8/PPP2PPP.text:
We're centralizing our knight and threatening to win material! 

It's borderline impossible to stop this. Test it out for yourself in the analysis!

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2pp4/5B2/8/PPP1NPPP/.text: Recapturing, but now Nc3 is very strong.

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppppp/1q3n2/2pP4/4P3/2N5/P1P.text: And we can establish our two central pawns. This idea will also be seen in the Ne4 & c5 Trompowsky!

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppppp/1q3n2/2pP4/5B2/8/PPP1P.text:
The immediate ...Qb6 attacks our b2 pawn.

But we'll just gambit it and develop our queen's knight!

We're not afraid of this capture because our development will be quicker than Black's, and the queen will be misplaced.

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppppp/1q3n2/2pP4/8/2N5/P1PBP.text: The queen returns from her trip to b2.

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2pP4/5B2/2N5/PqP1P.text:
Black takes. Our knight is attacked.

But we'll just retreat our bishop to d2, defending the knight. Black is going to have to waste time extricating their queen.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q1p1n2/2pP4/5B2/2N5/PP.text:
Defending c5, and opening up the light-squared bishop.

We'll defend the pawn with the queen.

If Black doesn't take on b2, we'll defend it. There's no need to give it away if they lose their chance.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/1q1p1n2/2pPp3/5B2/2N5/PP.text:
Placing a pawn in the center and attacking our bishop.

We'll attack the knight and threaten to take on f6, wrecking the structure.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/4P3/2N5/PPP.text:
Black castles.

We develop our bishop. 

Our bishop comes out first because we're controlling the g4-square, preventing ...Bg4.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3p1np1/2pPp3/4P3/2N3P1/P.text:
Black castles.

We'll fianchetto. Our central pawns are very strong.

rnbq1rk1/pp4b1/3p1np1/2pPpp2/4P3/2N3P1/P.text: Black recaptures. Our h-file is now open.

rnbq1rk1/pp4b1/3p1np1/2pPpp2/4P3/2N3PN/P.text:
And not only is our development smooth, but Black's counterplay is insufficient. 

We're coming closer with Qe2 and Ng5, with 0-0-0 to safeguard our king. It's hard to suggest moves for Black, since their development is cramped.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/3p1np1/2pPpp1P/4P3/2N3P1/.text:
The knight returns to the center, putting pressure on e4. 

We'll take on g6.

rnbqk2r/pp2bpp1/3p1n1p/2pPp3/4P3/2N5/PPP.text:
The queen had questionable usefulness on b6.

We'll check on b5. The point is we will either trade our bad bishop or disrupt black's coordination.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/8/2N5/PPPBPP.text:
Developing the bishop is the most popular and actually fairly logical.

Mostly, the bishop on e7 prevents a pin on f6 and it doesn't create weaknesses with a g6 fianchetto.

We'll expand in the center, with strong pawns.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4PB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black fianchettoes.

We'll give a check on b5, disrupting Black's coordination. 

The reasoning is that both queenside minor pieces have to be developed through d7, so when a piece blocks on d7, they'll be cramped.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/3p1np1/2pPp3/4P3/2N5/PPPB.text:
Black fianchettoes.

We'll fianchetto as well. 

Since it's a closed position, we need to find a logical square for our light-squared bishop. Playing Bb5+, helping Black trade a piece, doesn't make much sense.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/2pP4/4PB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black covers b5 and prepares ...b5 themselves.

But we can already force a better endgame by opening up the center, starting with the capture on e6.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/3p1n2/p1pP4/1p2PB2/P4P2/1.text: ...a5 adds another supporter, yet it's pinned, so we'll take on b4.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/3p1n2/p2P4/1p2PB2/2P2P2/1.text:
And we play another move to undermine the overextended queenside. 

If ...bxc3, we recapture with the knight and we've got Bb5+ ideas to develop with tempi on the Black pieces. After we get the bishop out, Nge2 will become possible.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/3p1n2/p2P4/1p2PB2/5P2/1PP.text: Black recaptures with the c-pawn. Taking with the a-pawn would have hung the rook!

rnbqkb1r/p2p1ppp/4p3/1ppP3n/8/5P2/PPP1P1.text:
...e6 to undermine our pawn. The queen is also unleashed.

We develop our knight on h3, where it neutralizes the queen check on h4.

rnbqkb1r/p2ppppp/5n2/1ppP4/5B2/8/PPP1PPP.text:
Black plays in the style of the Benko Gambit!

We'll play f3. Our idea is to build a strong center.

rnbqkb1r/p2ppppp/8/1ppP3n/5B2/5P2/PPP1P1.text:
Attacking our bishop...

We'll drop our bishop all the way back to c1.

rnbqkb1r/p3pppp/3p1n2/1ppP4/5B2/5P2/PPP1.text:
Fixing our pawn on d5.

We'll build our center with e4.

rnbqkb1r/p3pppp/3p1n2/2pP4/1p2PB2/5P2/PP.text:
Black continues expanding on the queenside.

We'll play to undermine them with a3.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2pP4/5B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
...e6 yet again undermines our pawn.

We can just support it with our knight.

We're not worried about ...exd5 as after Nxd5 we're threatening Nc7+.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
...c5 immediately undermines our center.

In order to avoid that attack, we'll push our pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2pP4/5B2/2N5/PPP.text:
The idea is to fianchetto.

We'll expand in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2pP4/5B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
...d6 is the most played move here. It fixes our d-pawn.

Let's develop, supporting our center.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/3p1np1/2pPp3/8/2N5/PPPBP.text:
The point is Black needs to develop the bishop somewhere.

On e7, it was blocked in by the d6 and c5 pawns.

We support our center. The center is locked, but since we have more space to develop our pieces we'll stand slightly better.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/5B2/2N5/PPP1.text:
Creating a triangle central pawn structure.

Even though this allows an en passant capture, en passant isn't forced. 

Let's just bring the bishop back.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/2pP4/5B2/2N5/PPP1P.text:
...d6 is a move that needs to be played in order to develop the dark-squared bishop without us attacking it with d6.

We add another pawn to support our center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black plays their hyper-modern move.

Our bishop comes out. This is the London!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to chapter nine on the London. We'll see some odd moves Black can play after 1...Nf6. 

In this first study, we'll stay in fairly normal territory with 2...c5. A logical move, undermining the center, after which we can push our pawn forward. 

Black,  depending on what they like to do, can go for many different setups against our 1.d4 and 2.Bf4. Let's learn how to deal with every one of them!

rnbqnrk1/pp3pbp/3p2p1/2pPp3/4P3/2N3P1/PP.text:
Black intends f5 for counterplay. 

Unfortunately, this means they're moving the same piece twice in the opening, while the queenside pieces haven't yet moved.

We can launch a pawn storm on the kingside, disregarding ...f5.

rnbqnrk1/pp4bp/3p2p1/2pPpp2/4P2P/2N3P1/P.text:
The intended f5, attacking the base of our center. 

We don't need to react defensively, however. We can just continue our attack with h5, undermining g6.

1rb1kb1r/p2npp1p/3p1np1/q1pP4/4P3/2N2N2/.text: The rook may retreat. This is logical.

1rb1kb1r/p2npp1p/3p1np1/q1pP4/P3P3/2N2N2.text:
And now we play a4 to secure our a2 weakness, and we're playing Be2 next to castle! 

We have superior space, and a timely knight move to attack the queen. After castling, we'll play Re1 and the e5 pawn break if allowed.

1rb1kb1r/p2npppp/3p1n2/q1pP4/5B2/2N2N2/P.text:
The rook may come to the semiopen file to attack the b-pawn. 

This is standard Benko-like compensation.

But we can unpin the knight, inviting ...Rxb2 stuff.

2b1kb1r/p2npp1p/3p1np1/q1pP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
Black will fianchetto their bishop. Where else could they go? However the light-squared bishop is still on c8.

We can attack the rook and form a battery, doing everything we can with tempi like we should in an opening.

2b1kb1r/p2npppp/3p1n2/q1pP4/8/2N2N2/PrPB.text:
If Black takes the pawn...

Our center is enviable and our development flows smoothly.

r1b1kb1r/p2npppp/3p1n2/qNpP4/5B2/5N2/PPP.text:
Check! Forking our pieces. 

But this doesn't work.

We can just retreat the knight to c3.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/2pp1np1/8/3P4/4PN1P/PP.text:
Black castles.

We play Be2. There is little point going to d3 after g6.

r1bqk2r/pp1nppbp/2pp1np1/8/3P1B2/4PN1P/P.text:
Black fianchettoes.

Let's go into our safe home, taking care of our bishop overseeing the e5 square.

r1bqkb1r/p2npppp/3p1n2/1ppP4/5B2/2N2N2/P.text:
Some players with Black like to push ...b5, thinking this pawn is always immune.

But we can just take it. It's not the Benko. Sometimes the pawn is just free.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp1p/2pp1np1/8/3P1B2/4PN2/P.text:
Black will fianchetto, since the e7 and d6 pawns stand in the way of the bishop.

We create a retreat square for our bishop: it controls the e5-square and helps prevent the ...e5 push. 

In the opening, we have to take care of our best pieces!

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2pp1n2/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Black develops as well. The idea of d6 might as well be to play ...e5 at some point.

Let's fight for control of e5, and continue to develop, by playing Nf3! 

If we work against Black's plan, we can make their setup backfire against them.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/3p1n2/2p5/3P1B2/2N2N2/.text:
Black undermines our d4 pawn.

But as is the case in many of these openings, sometimes we can just push the pawn and have more space.

e4 is coming to solidify our center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2np1n2/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
So maybe ...d6 to play e5 is the only unique thing they could throw at you.

But we'll develop our knight and control e5. If the entire opening revolves around ...e5 and we control it, Black is in trouble.

r1bqkb1r/pppnpppp/3p1n2/8/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1.text:
Black may insist on going for ...e5.

We'll discourage it by developing our knight to f3.

r1bqkb1r/pppppppp/2n2n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
This is another option. But after the most played ...d6, it'll just transpose into our early Nc6 chapter.

We continue normally and play e3.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2NP4/4PN1P.text:
We can attack d6 and add an attacker on e5! 

Black may try an ...e4 push followed by ...d5 to defend the attacked pawns, but our knight will be able to go to d6 either way, defended by our hidden bishop on h2.  

White has a slight edge.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/3P4/4PN1P/.text: ...e5 at last. But the pawn break isn't truly effective, considering our e3-d4 pawn structure is solid.

r1bqr1k1/pp1nppbp/2pp1np1/8/3P4/4PN1P/PP.text:
Black adds another supporter of e5.

We'll castle.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2np1n2/8/3P1B2/4Pb2/PPP.text:
Taking the knight to play e5 is futile...

After we recapture with the bishop, e5 would be a serious blunder given that we can take the knight on c6 with the bishop and simply win a pawn.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2np1n2/8/3P1Bb1/4PN2/PP.text:
Black pins us. This is the only chance they may have to play ...e5.

Yet we can unpin, and we'll invite ...Bxf3, giving us the bishop pair, in exchange for allowing ...e5.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2nppn2/8/3P1B2/4PB2/PPP2.text:
But after castling, we have the bishop pair and Black hasn't decided how they want to play in the center.

We can continue with c4 and Nc3, developing our pieces. Our bishops will prove advantageous in the long run.
That's why ...e6 would be the sound move.

rn1qkb1r/pbp1pppp/1p3n2/3p4/3P1B2/2P1PN2.text: Just remember to play the standard London moves you already know. You'll enjoy a nice advantage.

rn1qkb1r/pbp1pppp/1p3n2/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/P.text: If d5, or something entirely different (there are many possibilities not covered).

rn1qkb1r/pbpppppp/1p3n2/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
Black will fianchetto.

And after Nf3, should they go e6, we'll have transposed into the Nf6/e6 chapter. 

Remember that in that chapter you developed with Nc3 and jumping to b5.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/1qpp1np1/8/3P1B2/1PP1PN1.text:
And now we achieve our standard London pawn structure and block the bishop's diagonal.

We'll continue with Nbd2 (with Nc4 as a threat) and Qc2. Instead of Bd3 like in the London, we'll go Be2, since aiming at g6 with our bishop doesn't make much sense.

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppppp/1qp2n2/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Black can introduce this move.

But we push our b-pawn and defend our b2 weakness.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qpp1np1/8/3P1B2/1P2P2P.text:
Black will fianchetto their bishop. What else?

We'll develop our king's knight, adding further control to the e5 square.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qpp1n2/8/3P1B2/1P2P3/P.text:
Black may yet again try for ...e5.

We'll cover the g4 square and prevent Black from pinning our knight when we bring it to f3.

rnbqkb1r/p1pppppp/1p3n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Black will fianchetto. Ok, this might seem like something different, but if you play your standard London moves, you may notice Black may veer into something more familiar.

We'll continue with our usual e3.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2p2n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Now if Black goes ...d5 we'll transpose into a 1...d5 London.

We play our standard e3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2pp1n2/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
This, instead of ...d5, is a different setup we haven't seen. But it isn't particularly ambitious.

We'll develop our knight with Nd2.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p1n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PP.text:
Aiming directly for a future ...e5 is another possibility.

I suggest developing the knight quickly.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
Black develops their knight in a hyper-modern style.

Our bishop comes out in standard London fashion. And here's where Black starts to play unusually...

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
As foreshadowed by the title of this study, you guessed it, Black can throw at you moves that are completely random, possibly even bad after 1...Nf6. 

If this is the case, we'll be happy to see these moves be played! Let's just learn something to deal with them accordingly. We begin with 1.d4.

r1b1r1k1/ppppp1bp/B7/3N1p2/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
It should be a trivial win now.

I feel that our clever 4.h4 will take your opponent into unknown territory and you'll score many wins like this.

rnb1qrk1/ppp3bp/3pp3/5p1Q/2BP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
If they beg for a queen trade, we don't have to accept it here.

Since keeping the pressure is better, we'll move our queen away. h2 is a great square for her, keeping an eye on e5.

rnb1qrk1/ppppp1bp/8/5p1Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/PPP.text:
Black may be desperate for a queen trade. 

Normally this makes sense for the defending side, but here we have a neat tactical follow-up which means we're simply winning after the queens come off.

rnb1r1k1/ppppp1bp/8/5p2/3P1B2/2N1P3/PPP2.text:
Black recaptures.

But after Nd5, c7 is a weakness that cannot be defended. Note how little development Black has, and the row of unmoved pawns.

rnb2rk1/ppp3bp/3pp1q1/5p2/2BP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
The engine gives us a +2 advantage because of our activity. 

We have more than enough compensation for the exchange.
Black brings their queen to g6 to try and defend their king.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p4/5p1Q/3P1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
This natural move is a huge mistake.

Bc4 arrives with check! 

One of our pieces comes alive with a tempo.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3pp3/5p1Q/2BP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
The pawn blocks.

After Nf3, Black is in great trouble. 

All of our pieces are coming together in the attack.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/3P1B1P/2N1P3/.text:
Black castles.

We'll push forward, playing a classic breakthrough with h5. 

The idea is to open up the h-file with an exchange sacrifice.
